hall.d: Its biggest hall seats a thousand at one table, three hundred metres of it, made from forty block tables nobody would give up. Dishes travel the length by hand, under lids, and arrive warm.
Nobody lifts a lid until the cook calls 'lids', and then four hundred come up at once. In heliox the ring carries the length of the arcade, and latecomers start to run.

The drum's biggest choir has three thousand voices in three shifts, lamp-dawn, evening and lamp-night, and the shifts sing together only on Booking Day. The lamp-night shift thinks it is the best, and says so quietly.

On Booking Day every block choir sings its own year from the Ledger: each newborn's name beside the name of the dead whose share they carry, two names to a phrase. A block has about twenty-five pairs, so it takes ten minutes, and nobody leaves early.
Its opera is famous for basses. Heliox brightens every voice, so a bass who still sounds dark has trained for a decade, and the house hangs its felt three layers deep so you can hear what they won.
One motion, four speakers, and the audience votes by walking to one end of the hall or the other. The motions are kept, and the one about lighting the Court has come up forty-one times.

A terrace on the back end wall is kept for dancing at a third of a g, where a leap hangs long enough to turn in. Every leap lands a hand's width spinward, so the reels are written to travel, and a dance that ends where it began was danced wrong.
Its puppet house works with the air: a whisper behind the screen reaches the back row, so nobody ever shouts. The figures are cut from remade card, and each is lit by one hand lamp.

buy.item: a shadow puppet, cut to order

hall.d: When a long letter lands from across the Shade, years on the way, the hall reads it aloud to anyone who comes, with the addressee's leave. The writer may have died since, so a chair is left empty at the front.

Children here are taught in halls of three hundred by a dozen teachers at once, each with a corner, and they wander between corners as their questions take them. It costs the drum a great many hours, and its children argue better than anyone's.
Anyone may tell, nobody may tell the same story twice in a year, and the oldest teller in the room goes last. On a good night it runs until the laundry starts.
Its hall quiz has run every {weekday} for two hundred years, and every question must be answerable without compute. Teams tie black threads on for the evening, and the prize is a tomato.

buy.item: a printed book of old questions

hall.d: Its chess club meets in a flying hall in the lamp-night, players tethered either side of the board at under 3% of a g. A dropped rook drifts off so slowly that the loser has time to apologise to it.

Every block has a string quartet that plays on Fridays for whoever comes, on instruments with bodies deeper than old pictures show, built to sound warm in a bright air. The hall pays all four, and nobody thinks four people's evening is too dear.

One hall on the Quaysides has served without shutting for three hundred years; in the Eleven Days it handed out its larder by hand lamp. Back crews, Gate night shifts and wanderers off the late glides all eat there.

Every guest on guest-right is asked to cook one dish from home, once, on a night they choose. The best go on the hall's card with the guest's drum beside them, and the card now runs to six hundred dishes.

buy.item: a print of the guests' card

hall.d: On {weekday}s each volunteer brings one family dish, unlabelled, and the table guesses whose aunt made what. Guessing wrong is a small disaster; guessing right is how you get asked back.
Every hall has a song for when the stew comes out, some so old the words have worn smooth. Nobody knows any more why the Ring {ring} hall's song is about a cab that wouldn't lean.

A cook called {name}, ninety-four, still makes the morning jook in the hall by Station Ring {ring}. {name} salts by taste from the ladle and won't write it down, so three apprentices stand alongside, tasting.
Any child of twelve may apprentice in a hall kitchen a few hours a week, paid like anyone else. Half the drum's cooks started that way, and all of them can cut a jelly cube square without looking.
Its halls are judged by their ceilings, hung with felt in the block's colours and re-dyed every Booking Day for a few kays. You can eat at a table of four hundred and still hear the person opposite.

buy.item: a felt panel in this year's colours

hall.d: Its theatre plays on a terrace at a third of a g, where an actor can leap onto a table from the floor and a fall from a balcony is a slow joke. Tragedies struggle there: the dead come down too gently.
Its comedy hall has one rule: every joke must work in heliox, so nothing leans on a deep voice. The house favourite, older than anyone in the audience, is a man trying to pour tea crosswise.

Dumplings are folded at the table: wrappers come round, you fill and fold, and twenty minutes later the steamer comes back with everyone's dumplings, known by their pleats. Children's pleats are the easiest to spot and the first to go.

Each hall keeps a stockpot on the 65 °C loop that is never boiled and never emptied, topped up with each day's trimmings and herb stalks. The oldest claims four hundred years, and the inspectors have stopped arguing.

buy.item: a jar of stock from the oldest pot

hall.d: Its Booking Day feast spends most of the Quiet's savings on salad: bowls of it, cut generously, more green than most people see in a year. The oldest cooks make it and the youngest serve it.
On the Quiet each hall makes its soup by passing the pot down the table, every household adding one thing from its larder. It is usually strange and always finished.

Its choirs keep a book of every song received in a Passing over six hundred years, and sing one at every Homecoming. Some came from rafts long since gone out of earshot, which will never hear an answer.

buy.item: a printed book of the passing songs

hall.d: New parents bring their baby to the block hall for its first taste of anything, a fingertip of the Nine, and the whole table watches the face. The hall's book records each face in one word.
Its halls cook for the elders who can't come down: lidded tins go up the lift cores every evening by cab, each with a note from whoever cooked it. Some elders reply on the lid.
Each hall rings a hand bell for dinner, every bell tuned to its own note, bright in the heliox. Children learn the halls by their notes before they learn their numbers.
Its halls fry sour-starch crepes in the lamp-night, when kWh are cheapest, and sell them to the night crews at half the evening price. The griddles go cold at lamp-dawn and the queue goes with them.
Every hall makes its own chilli crisp, and the blind tasting on the Quiet has gone to the same hall nine years running. The others say it's the black garlic and are trying hard not to copy it.

buy.item: a jar of the winning chilli crisp

hall.d: Its block choirs swap one singer a month, so a voice from the Low decks sings with a High-deck choir for a while and comes home with all their news. It's how the drum learns what it's thinking.

Once a year every choir in the drum sings the same round, entering by the clock one station ring after another, so the tune runs the length of the drum. Ring 9 finishes eleven minutes after Ring 1, and complains.

buy.item: a print of the round's score

hall.d: Its circus works the end-wall terraces at a quarter of a g, where a flyer hangs a full second at the top of a throw. Catchers learn to stand a hand's width spinward of where it looks right.
At a naming the child's table lifts twelve lids, one dish at a time, and under the last lid is a herb cutting for the child's first shelf. Basil is usual; mint is considered a joke.

buy.item: a basil cutting in a paper pot

hall.d: Its halls trade cooks with drums on the far side of Merrow for a year at a time, by slow cycler, and every menu shows who's visiting. This year's borrowed cook is from {far} and has opinions about salt.
Food cools four times faster in heliox, so the halls' favourite dinner is hot pot: one pot to six people, kept at a simmer on its own plate. Whoever takes the last piece pays the cook's tip.
Its theatres stage plays of exactly thirty minutes, timed so shift crews can see one between the cab and dinner. Eleven run at once in eleven rooms, and regulars manage three a night.
Its brass band plays horns nearly twice the old length, coiled tight to fit the arcades, and marches antispinward because it's a little lighter going. Coming back, it takes a cab.
Its hall school takes sixty students a year from anywhere on Merrow and lends them Margin flats for the course. Each leaves with a good knife and a spoon of the school's starter.

buy.item: a spoon of the school's starter

hall.d: Once a year its theatre plays a recording made in the old air, long before the drums, and the whole house hears it through a blanket. Children laugh at the low voices, then go quiet halfway through.

A stair climbs six decks round an atrium, and on festival nights a choir stands on every landing and sings to the one above. In heliox the echo comes back sooner than anyone expects, and the parts are written to land in it.
Its halls sing a four-bar grace in four parts before dinner, and the lids stay down until the chord ends. A hall that drifts out of tune eats its first course in silence.
Its reading hall reads one long book aloud a chapter a night, and a reader who stumbles hands it to the next person along. They are three hundred nights into something nobody remembers choosing.
A cellar hall serves only ferments, miso, pickles, lactic sours and cheese, all aged on the waste-heat loop. Children are allowed in once they can say 'lactic' with a straight face.
After dinner every guest is asked to teach the hall one song from home, and the hall sings it straight back. Some songs are now sung more often here than in the drums they came from.
Heliox lifts every whistle nearly an octave, so the yearly whistling contest goes to whoever can whistle lowest. The champion is a retired Gate clerk who sounds like a slow kettle.
Its music hall lets anyone join the band for one tune if they bring an instrument and keep time. The house players have learned to make room for a 1.2 m flute coming in sideways.
Its theatre stages the same play about the Eleven Days every year, lit by one hand lamp per actor. The last cast member who lived through it retired last year, at ninety-one.

Morning jook comes with a counter of thirty toppings, and regulars are known by their order. 'Black garlic, chilli crisp, two cubes' is a woman on deck {deck} who has had it most mornings for eighty years.

buy.item: a jar of hall black garlic

hall.d: Its halls serve on plates mended in plain sight, every crack filled with a line of coloured lacquer, and the most-mended plate goes to the guest of honour. Some plates are more seam than plate.

The drum's hall recipes are public and numbered, twelve thousand of them, so asking for a four-eighty at any counter gets you the same red stew. The argument about four-eighty-one is older than most halls.

buy.item: a printed index of the numbered recipes

hall.d: Weddings are held at the block's long table, and the apple is cut by the oldest person present, whoever that is. Couples have been known to invite a stranger of a hundred and three for the honour.

On the Long Flight its halls keep lidded broth hot all lamp-night for flyers coming down off the Spindle, chilled through by heliox at speed. You hand in your sleeves at the door and get them back with a cup.
Its dessert hall makes one Mill sweet a day, halwa, lokum, mochi or pulled sugar, and you can tell the weekday by the queue. On pulled-sugar days it goes round the block.

buy.item: a box of the day's sweets

hall.d: Its bakers proof on the 65 °C loop through the evening and bake in the lamp-night, when kWh are cheapest, so the halls' bread comes out at three in the morning. Night crews get the heels.

Every hall posts its accounts by the door: the cook's hours, the kitchen's kWh and what the volunteers ate. When a hall runs over, its regulars vote on the menu, and the vote always goes to less salad and more pastry.
Naming dinners here are huge: the child's table, the block, and at the head the family of the dead whose share the child carries, with a remade heirloom. The two families often stay friends for life.
Children argue in public from the age of nine, at a children's court held in the block atrium every week. The drum's adults are famous across {row} for being impossible to beat in an argument.

Anyone may pin a question on the hall's board and anyone may answer it at dinner, for a free bowl. The oldest open question is why a dropped cup lands anti; every child in the drum has had a go, and none has won the bowl.
Its halls seat everyone by lot at the door, family or not, so dinner is with whoever the draw gives you. Several marriages, two feuds and one choir have started at seat forty-one.
A choir of aunts, all over seventy, sings at every naming in its block and has done for fifty years. They know every child's name in the block and most of their faults.
It is polite to scrape your bowl here, and hall spoons are cut square at the tip to do it properly. Leaving food is read as a comment on the cook.
Every spinball match in the block leagues ends in the hall, where the losing side cooks for both teams. The best cooks in the drum play for its worst teams.

buy.item: a spinball signed by the losing cooks

hall.d: On the High decks a rota of children serves lunch to the elders, paid in pastry and stories. Years later the elders who are left turn out at the station ring for each of those children's Homecoming.
In the hall by each station ring, tea is poured by whoever arrived last, and newcomers are taught the hall's pour on their first night. Wanderers on guest-right leave knowing a dozen pours.
Once a month its biggest hall turns its lamps low and eats to a quartet. Nobody speaks, and the lids come off between movements.
Each Booking Day the young couples in lent Margin flats cook one dinner together for the block that lent them, and the block judges it out loud. It is always too ambitious and always forgiven.

wood.d: Its wood is yews, the oldest planted before anyone's oldest chair, kept by woodwardens who clip them by hand in the lamp-night. Yew grows slowly anywhere and slower in dim light, which suits a drum in no hurry.
Its birches are given a chilled-tent winter one strip at a time, so somewhere in the wood leaves are always yellowing and coming down. Every child may throw one armful, once, and remembers it.
A moss wood covers the dim end of the Hollow floor, where the sunline stops short and the light falls away. It is so soft underfoot that people leave their shoes at the edge in long rows.

Its parks are woods lit to a thousand lux instead of bright squares at ten thousand, which spreads the same lamps over ten times the ground. Every block has a dim wood the size of a field, and nobody in it hurries.
A bamboo wood whose stalks knock softly together when the air handlers change pace at lamp-night. The wardens say they can tell the hour by the knock, and crop the canes for paper and chopsticks.

One atrium wood is kept at dusk-light all day, never brighter than the last half hour of a painted dusk, and planted with hazel and ferns that like it that way. People stand at the gate until their eyes catch up.
A wood of junipers, kept for the smell, and every visitor asks about gin. The wardens explain that gin is made in the Mill from milligrams of pinene, and that the junipers are for looking at.

buy.item: a sprig of juniper in a paper twist

wood.d: Willows line a slow canal whose water moves only because pumps move it, their tips trailing in it. Wardens trim them from the bank with a pole and give the withies to the basket-makers.

A hazel coppice is cut in rotation for poles, hoops and stakes for the Garden racks, so some patch is always freshly cut and bright. The record of which stool was cut when goes back four hundred years.

An atrium of tree ferns taller than two decks, chosen because ferns want so little light that the whole wood costs less to keep lit than one block's bright square. It smells of wet stone, and nobody knows why.
Its pear wood is pollinated by children with brushes, a class at a time, in silence, because the wardens say the trees don't care for chatter. Nobody believes this, and everybody whispers.
Cedars grow on the end-wall terraces, spreading in flat tiers like the terraces under them, and the whole wall smells of pencils. Wardens climb them at a third of a g and come down slowly.

Its figs set fruit without anyone's help, a rare thing in a drum with no bees, so the fig wood is the one orchard nobody has to brush. The figs go round by lottery, and the oldest warden gets the first.

When two people fill a slate between them in the wood, they may give it to the slate library, which copies it and wipes it clean. There are millions, and reading strangers' conversations is a whole afternoon's pleasure.
Woodwardens carry a small bell with one low note and ring it twice a day, at lamp-dawn and lamp-night; it is the only sound the wood makes on purpose. Children guess which warden by the ring.
Its wood halls serve supper in silence, lids lifted without a clink, with one slate passed along the table for anything that can't wait. Guests usually last two nights before laughing at something.
Margin flats at the wood's edge are lent for silent retreats of three to thirty days. You must bring a slate, and you must leave behind everything you wrote on it.

Children spend one morning a week in the wood school, which teaches silence the way other drums teach swimming: in short lengths, building up. By ten they can sit an hour; by twelve most of them like it.

The oldest tree in the drum is a yew of about nine hundred years, whose warden's post has passed through eleven people. Children may touch it twice: on their first visit, and on the day they leave on their wander year.

Wardens pick mushrooms from the moss and the strain library checks every basket; they are the only food in the drum that nobody planted. A plate at the wood hall costs less than a tomato and tastes of the floor.

buy.item: a paper bag of moss mushrooms

wood.d: In the wood, with nobody talking, you can hear the drum: fans, pumps, water, a faint tick as a duct cools. Wardens keep a slate of new noises, and a squeak noted in the wood reaches the Keel crews within the hour.
Wardens ask everyone to walk the wood's loop antispinward, the slightly lighter way, so nobody ever meets anyone head on. Walking it the other way is not forbidden, but people look.

Its wood covers the far side of the Hollow floor, so from the lawns opposite you look up into it, upside down and perfectly sharp. On a quiet afternoon you can watch a warden at work three kilometres overhead.

A wood climbs the end-wall terraces tier by tier, and near the top, at a twentieth of a g, the trees grow toward the light with nothing much pulling them down. Wardens tie them in with cord and patience.
Its orchard wood of old, unpruned apple trees gives a few thousand apples a year, and every one goes to a wedding, drawn by lot. Couples who win one cut it twice as carefully as anyone else.
Woodwarden is a childless calling here with the standing of a judge: a warden's slate can close a path for a month, and nobody argues with it out loud.
Everyone carries a slate, and a slate held face down means don't write to me. The drum's teenagers have built a whole language of slate angles that their parents can't read.

buy.item: a slate, remade, with a stick of chalk

wood.d: In the lamp-night the wood is lit only by hand lamps held low, and wardens walk the paths for anyone lost. Most of the people who get lost meant to.
The tallest bamboo is cut for flutes 1.2 m long, in silence, and the drum's flute-makers say a stalk that heard talking warps. They are joking, mostly, and still won't cut near the paths.
Wardens keep a seed library of every tree in the wood and give a seed to each child at their naming. The child plants it at twelve, and the wardens find room for the ones that live.
Fallen birch leaves are pulped and pressed into a soft grey paper for long letters, and every sheet keeps a leaf or two whole. Letters on it are written slowly, because the leaves get in the way.
Shadows in the wood never move, since the sunline doesn't; they only deepen and lift with the painted dawn and dusk. Wardens tell the time by how dark the shade under the yews has grown.
One day in ten the whole drum keeps silence in public, cabs, halls and Quaysides too. The Gate is the only place you may speak, and the Gate staff say it is like being famous.
On the anniversary of a death, families write to the dead on a slate, hang it in the yews for a week, then wipe it. The wardens read none of them and could recite most.
Its baths open onto the dim wood through a glass wall, and there is no talking in the water. In heliox even a drip carries, so you can hear the whole bath's breathing slow down.
The drum's grandest wedding gift is a sapling from the wood, planted by the couple where a warden says. It goes on the warden's slate under both their names for as long as it stands.

Its choir sings once a year, in the wood at lamp-dawn, and rehearses the rest of the year on slates and in its head. People say the one performance is worth the wait, which is the polite thing to say.
The drum has a sign language older than its halls, used in the wood and anywhere else quiet. Guests pick up 'thank you', 'jook' and 'which way is the lift' by their second night.

buy.item: a card of the commonest hand-signs

wood.d: Its wardens climb at half a g, higher and more slowly than anyone's, and their apprentices learn on the top-terrace trees, where a fall takes long enough to say something rude on the way down.
Under the yews is a box-hedge maze where talking is allowed only at the dead ends. Children run it as a race to be first to a dead end with something to say.
Personal compute doesn't reach the wood: the drum keeps it dark of signals, so walking in is going dark for an hour. People tie a black thread at the gate and untie it on the way out.
One day a year the wardens cut bamboo shoots and the halls serve them, the only fresh vegetable in the drum that costs nothing. Families queue at lamp-dawn and argue about how long to blanch them.

Old slates left on the wood's benches grow moss, and the drum's oldest conversation, left there three hundred years ago, is now unreadable and protected. Visitors write their guesses on their own slates.
The wood nearest the High decks is kept for elders at lamp-dawn: benches every fifty metres, no steps, and a warden who knows everyone's name and says none of them aloud.
Its birches are tapped for one week a year, and the sap is reduced slowly on the 65 °C loop into a thin, sharp syrup. Every household gets a spoonful, and guests may buy a little bottle.

buy.item: a small bottle of birch syrup

wood.d: Wood weddings are silent: the couple write their vows on one slate, and the apple is cut so quietly you can hear the knife meet the board. The clapping afterwards is the loudest thing in the wood all year.
Fallen yew is the only wood here anyone may take, and the drum's carvers turn it into small lidded boxes, one a day, in silence. Each box carries the date its branch came down.
The lowest tier of the end wall, where the light is weakest, is all moss and fern, and children roll down it at half a g. The wardens re-lay whatever gets flattened and pretend to be cross.
Its cabs carry a slate on the wall and no speakers, so stops are shown, not called. The arrival chime is a soft click you would miss in any other drum.
In the middle of the wood is a clearing kept at a hundred lux, about a room's evening light, where the drum's elders go to sit. It is the most asked-for place in the drum and the cheapest to light.

fair.d: Students compose dawns on a model sunline the length of a corridor, a hundred metres of lamps they can run at any speed. Each graduate gets one real dawn over the Hollow, played once, and the whole drum turns out to judge it.

Any resident may enter the yearly draw to paint one dawn. Last year's winner was a pipe-fitter of seventy who had planned his in a notebook since he was twelve, and it stayed grey for a whole hour on purpose.

Once a year {painter}, the drum's oldest lamp-painter, plays again the first dawn they ever made, changed a little each time. Families keep notebooks of the changes and argue about them until the next one.

Seats on the end-wall terraces for the evening shows go at auction, and the rents come back to every resident as a line on the wallet marked 'terraces'. People who never bid still check it, to see what kind of week the shows had.

buy.item: a terrace seat for one dusk, at auction

fair.d: A square of fountains whose jets climb twice as high as the same pumps could throw them at the rim, and take twice as long to fall. The tallest comes down a few metres spinward of its own nozzle, so its basin is built off-centre.

Water let go from a third-g terrace takes nearly twenty seconds to reach the floor 500 m below, and the drum turns under it all the way down, so the fall leans antispinward like a curtain pulled aside. The spinward side of its pool stays dry enough for picnics.

One day a year the end-wall terraces are given over to kites. At a third of a g a light kite stays up at a brisk walk, so families walk theirs along the tiers in slow processions, and on the top tiers people fly kites the size of rooms.

Once a week in the lamp-night the open Spindle is given over to the parade: thousands of flyers with hand lamps keeping one long line down the axis, end wall to end wall. Crossing the line is the rudest thing you can do up there, and also the hardest.

The floor's beds are planted upside down on purpose, so they read the right way up from the far bank, three kilometres overhead. Standing among them you see stripes of thyme and red chard; from across the Hollow they're this year's picture, a giant pear.

A yew maze on the floor, fiendish from inside and obvious from the far bank hanging three kilometres over it. Strangers up there send the lost directions by message, and some of them lie, which is half the fun.

Once a year the whole drum re-dyes in a colour drawn by lot at the block courts: coats, linings, market canopies, the felt in the halls. A re-dye costs about a tenth of a kWh, so even the oldest coat on the row comes out saffron.

buy.item: a packet of this year's dye

fair.d: A long lake kept glass-still, with no swimming until lamp-noon, so it holds a perfect copy of the far bank. Lie on the jetty and you see the drum twice, once overhead and once underfoot, and most people get dizzy and stay anyway.

A garden open only in the lamp-night, planted with pale flowers and lit from below by thousands of lamps of a watt or two each. Couples book its benches weeks ahead, and the gardeners have learned not to ask.

buy.item: a booked hour on a night-garden bench

fair.d: An acrobats' school on the third-g terraces, where a somersault lasts long enough to wave in the middle of it. Every catch is made a hand's width spinward of where a stranger would reach, and the troupe's children learn that before their letters.

Bamboo-and-felt puppets four storeys tall walk the terraces on four handlers each, which at a third of a g is plenty. On the drum's founding day they come down to the floor, where at half a g they lurch like tired uncles.

buy.item: a hand puppet sewn from the workshop's offcuts

fair.d: On festival nights a choir sings from the near bank and another answers from the far bank, three kilometres overhead. In heliox the sound takes about five seconds to cross, so the pieces are written around the gap, and the silence before each answer is part of the score.

Its Long Flight is the biggest on {row}: flyers go up in shifts from dusk to lamp-dawn, and the hand lamps along the axis are so thick that people on the floor say the sunline has come back on in pieces.

Every Booking Day the drum votes whether to keep its two extra hours of full sun or spend them on something else, and every year it keeps them. Neighbours claim they can spot its people by the squint.

Seats on the back terraces for a famous painter's dawn are auctioned months ahead and the rents shared out to everyone. The painter gets nothing extra, by custom, except the first coffee of the morning from every cart on the terrace.

buy.item: a back-terrace seat for a famous dawn

fair.d: Pumps drive a fast channel over a hump in the floor so that one wave stands in place, tall and slow at half a g. Surfers queue on the bank with numbered tickets, and the record ride, fifty-one minutes, belongs to a woman of eighty-two.

A water organ at the foot of the end wall, run off the fountain pumps, with pipes nearly twice as long as they'd need in old air. It plays every dusk, and the tune changes whenever the elders lose an argument to the children.

Once a month the sunline plays a whole day in a single colour drawn from a hat at the block courts: a green day, an amber day, one long-remembered violet. It costs almost nothing, and people date their memories by them.

One morning a year the sunline is lit red at one end, green in the middle and blue at the other, so every shadow on the floor comes in three colours. Children spend the whole morning chasing their own.

Couples marry in the flying halls at under 3% of a g, guests hanging in a ring around them with hand lamps. The apple is cut crosswise in the air, and the halves are passed so carefully that no seed drifts off.

In the last minutes of dusk, when the Spindle opens, flyers carry great bamboo-and-paper cut-outs close to the dimming sunline, and their shadows walk across the floor a kilometre and a half below. The story changes every year; the giant never does.

Every lamp-noon forty flyers in coloured sleeves cross the flying hall in formation, each aiming wide so the Coriolis bend brings them all through the same hoop. When one misses, the crowd groans, which in heliox sounds like a kettle.

buy.item: an hour's lesson in hoop flying

fair.d: In the lamp-night the lake is lit from below in slow colours, and swimmers float on their backs at half a g looking up at the dark far bank, where the night walkers' hand lamps move like beads on a string.

A walk of hanging glass prisms near the back end wall throws bands of colour across the floor at full sun. The bands never move, since the sunline doesn't, and the drum's lamp-painters come here to steal ideas from a picture that holds still.

Every dawn and dusk the drum's painters have played in four hundred years, kept as files and replayed on request under a small dome on the back terraces. Copies are free; a seat costs a fifth of a kWh, for the cushions.

buy.item: a seat in the dawn library

fair.d: Once a year the dawn is painted by the drum's schoolchildren, a minute each, so it jumps from lilac to orange to a sudden dark and back. Everyone calls it the worst dawn of the year, and nobody misses it.

On the top terraces, where almost nothing weighs anything and the air barely stirs, soap bubbles as big as a child hang for minutes. Children blow them from hoops on poles while the old keep the times, and the record is chalked on the wall.

buy.item: a bubble hoop on a bamboo pole

fair.d: Once a year everyone with a window on the end-wall terraces lights it in the same colour at the same minute, and the whole wall changes at once. The cheer from the wall reaches the floor a few seconds after the light does.
Each tier of the back end wall is planted in one colour of flower, deep violet at the foot and paler with every tier, to white at the top. People say the wall gets lighter in both senses.

buy.item: a packet of violet seeds from the bottom tier

fair.d: Once a year the drum pays out its Hollow and terrace rents in one lump instead of monthly, and everyone spends it the same week: a relining, an apple, a dinner cooked by someone else. The tailors are booked solid and take their own holiday the week after.

A public stair climbs the back end wall from the floor to the flying halls, lighter with every step until the last flights feel like climbing in a dream. Most people stop for tea at the third-g tier and ride the Spindle lift the rest of the way.

buy.item: a pot of tea at the third-g tier

fair.d: A swing on a twenty-metre rope hangs from a gantry on the quarter-g terraces, and each swing there and back takes eighteen seconds. There is always a queue, and a good share of the drum's proposals happen at the top of the arc.
A path across the floor lit a different colour every ten metres, walked slowly in the lamp-night by people who have just lost someone. Nobody explains it to visitors; they find out by walking it.

A great clock of flower beds on the floor, planted with flowers that open and close on the sunline's ramp, so the hours show as colour. Its keepers say it keeps better time than the lamp clock, which is what sets the sunline in the first place.

A street of lamp-painters' studios on deck {hdeck}, each with a model sunline down its ceiling, where you can sit in while a dawn is built a minute at a time. The painters let anyone watch and glare at anyone who asks when it will be ready.

Every dusk an orchestra plays on the floor under the dimming sunline, timed so the last chord lands as the light goes. Its brass is nearly twice the length of the instruments in old pictures, and carries right up the end walls.

Four times a year the floor's paths and benches are painted with a glow paint that drinks in the sunline all day and gives it back in the lamp-night, faint green and blue. It wears off in a week, and the children sulk until the next one.

Flyers trail long dyed ribbons through the netted flying halls, and because every crosswise pass bends, the ribbons draw curves nobody could draw by hand. Pictures of the best are pinned up in the lift lobbies with the flyers' names.

buy.item: a ten-metre flying ribbon, dyed to order

fair.d: At half a g stilts can be twice the old height, and the festival walkers on the floor stride past the pavilions' upper windows. They lean into every turn, since a step spinward lands heavier than a step anti.

buy.item: an afternoon's hire of festival stilts

fair.d: On festival nights the painters light the far half of the Hollow's floor in slow washes of colour while the near half stays dark. Lying on your back on the near side, you seem to be looking down into a lit bowl.

Every evening a lawn on the floor lights one small lamp for each child born that day, about four thousand, each marked with the child's two names. Families walk the rows after dinner to find theirs, and strangers stop to read the pairs.

A jumping pit on the top terraces where a child can clear the height of a house and an adult two. Every jumper comes down a little spinward of the mark, so the target is painted crooked, and visitors still land on the wrong side of it.

On the drum's founding day the Hollow rota is set aside and anyone may go up, so the floor fills shoulder to shoulder and the far bank looks like a carpet with people in it. The pavilions give away cake until it runs out, usually by ten.

On Homecoming night each returned wanderer floats a lamp on the lake, a watt in a paper cup, and their tables stand along the jetty counting them in. The youngest aunts gather the cups up next morning.

buy.item: a lamp in a paper cup

fair.d: A market in the flying-hall lobby re-dyes wing-sleeves while you wait, in any of three hundred colours, so the halls are full of flyers who couldn't decide. The colour costs a tenth of a kWh; the rest is twenty minutes of the dyer's patience.

buy.item: a wing-sleeve re-dye while you wait

fair.d: On festival days one flying hall takes down its inner nets and anyone may step off the Spindle lift's top platform into the air. At under 3% of a g you drift down to the outer net over most of half a minute, slowly enough to wave to everyone you know.

The Booking Day question here is always about light: a longer dusk, a brighter lamp-night on the paths, a dawn in colour every Sunday. 'Colour on Sundays' won by two points last year, and the painters' waiting list now runs to a decade.

A tier of the front end wall is faced with polished panels that throw the Hollow's glow back across the floor, so the floor by that wall never gets the usual dim end. The flats behind it are let at auction, and the rents shared out, as everything is here.

In the lamp-night old films are shown on a great screen on the far bank, upside down so they read right from below, with the sound sent to everyone's ear. The old recordings sound spoken through a blanket, and the whole floor says the famous lines along with them.

Once a year the sunline is masked at lamp-noon for twelve minutes, and the whole Hollow goes dim in the middle of full sun. Elders call it a rehearsal for the Dark; the children treat it as a game of hide and seek.

A spiral slide runs down the back end wall from the third-g tier to the floor, lazy at the top and fast at the bottom, with every turn banked for the Coriolis lean. It takes four minutes, and adults in the queue say they're only there for the children.

One evening a year two lamp-painters split a dusk, one taking the front half of the sunline and one the back, and the terraces vote by raising hand lamps. The loser buys the winner a single tomato, in front of everyone.

Divers go off a tower at the lake's edge, taking half again as long to fall at half a g, and the judges score them on what they fit into the extra time. The best turn so slowly at the top that the crowd counts their rotations aloud.

Folded paper gliders launched from the top terraces stay up for minutes in the low weight and drift down the end wall in long curls, bending antispinward as they go. The gardeners gather them up by the basket for the remake bins.
At the first minute of Booking Day's dawn everyone on the floor raises a hand lamp, block after block round the drum, so a ring of light runs right round the Hollow and meets itself overhead.

Each year the drum lends one dusk to a wanderer on guest-right, drawn by lot from the guest flats, who paints it with a lamp-painter's help in three nights. Some of the strangest dusks in the files came from twenty-year-olds who had never touched a sunline.

maker.d: A chair school where every apprentice's test piece is a grandparent's chair, taken apart and made sound again. New wood is the last resort: a new chair costs 125 kays, and the masters say so often.

buy.item: a child's stool, remade from offcuts

maker.d: Sagging armchairs arrive by freight from rows away to be re-sprung, and wait their turn in a long hall with tickets tied to their arms. The springs are remade from old ones, so the bill is almost all hours.

Furniture built for the high decks and the Hollow pavilions, where a sitter weighs barely half what they would at the rim, so a chair needs a third less wood. Take one down to the Low decks and it creaks at you.
The Hollow's birch prunings come down from the woodwardens once a month and leave as bowls, each signed on the foot with the tree it came from. The lathes run all that week.
Stools of Hollow bamboo, lashed rather than glued, light enough to carry up a terrace stair in one hand. Every block hall on the row has a stack of them, and no two match.

The long tables of cooked halls all over the row are built here, in leaves that bolt together so a hall can seat four hundred or forty. Old leaves come back to be planed, and some have been round a dozen halls.

buy.item: a cutting board planed from an old table leaf

maker.d: Its cradles are lent, never sold: each goes from naming to naming and comes back with another child's name cut into the rail. The oldest carries forty-one names and its eleventh pair of rockers.
Pictures in wood inlay, cut from the offcuts of remade chairs, so every panel is made of other people's furniture. The school's great piece is a map of the drum in two hundred shades of offcut.

Rocking chairs curved for the weight they'll carry, because a rocker's pace changes with the deck: one made for deck 150 dawdles up near the Hollow and rattles on the Low decks. Buyers give their deck number before their name.

buy.item: a rocking chair for your deck, remade

maker.d: New feet for old chairs, turned while you wait from offcuts of the right wood. The turners read the wear before they start, and can usually tell you which way the last owner leaned.

buy.item: four chair feet, turned to match

maker.d: Flutes of Hollow bamboo, 1.2 metres and longer, cut and tuned in the drum's own air. {name}, who has fitted players for fifty years, measures your arms before looking at your hands.

In heliox a horn needs nearly twice the tubing to sound the same note, so these coil three times round and weigh more than old pictures suggest. The brass is all remade, and the makers keep a list of which door handles went into which horn.

A child's first instrument here is a recorder cut to heliox length, about sixty centimetres, so it comes up to their chin. Most are lent, played for a few years, and brought back with the tooth marks sanded off.

Hand drums with bodies twice as deep as the old patterns, since a drum's boom lives in the air inside it and heliox pushes it up. The heads are vat-grown membrane, warmed on the 65 °C loop and left a week to settle.

buy.item: a frame drum with a vat-grown head

maker.d: Its bells are cast from remade metal and ring on for half a minute, because the thin air takes their note away slowly. Each is tuned against a fork, since a bell's pitch lives in the metal and doesn't care what air it's in.

Lutes and fiddles with bellies like barrels, because a soundbox has to grow to keep its warmth when the air carries sound so fast. Strings take an hour; a body takes a year, and the queue for one takes longer.

Its organ-builders supply halls across the row, and their own organ climbs a six-deck atrium, because in heliox the lowest pipe needs eighteen metres to sound. Children may sit inside the case while it plays, once.

buy.item: a whistle cut from a retired pipe

maker.d: A fork rings at the same pitch in any air, which makes it the one honest judge in a drum where every flute is a compromise. The workshop here remakes them from old cutlery and sends them out in felt-lined cases.

buy.item: a tuning fork in a felt case

maker.d: Pan pipes of Hollow bamboo cut to heliox lengths, so the longest tube of a set reaches a child's waist. Every child here cuts a set of their own at eight, and the crooked ones are kept.

buy.item: a set of bamboo pan pipes

maker.d: Music boxes with combs of remade steel, each pinned with one tune: a naming song, a wedding reel, the drum's own lamp-dawn call. A comb's note is in its metal, so they play the same tunes here as in the oldest recordings.

buy.item: a music box pinned with a tune you choose

maker.d: Wing-sleeves cut wide and slow for elders who want to fly the Long Flight without hurrying anyone. The fins run from wrist to knee, and the makers fit them sitting down, with tea.

Narrow sleeves for racing the length of the Spindle in the lamp-night, stiffened at the cuff so a flyer can steer with a turn of the wrist. They're useless crosswise, which the makers say is the point.

buy.item: a pair of racing sleeves, remade

maker.d: Half the flying halls within twenty glides are netted from here: kilometres of vat-fibre mesh, checked by hand a knot at a time. Retired net becomes string bags, and every slow-line galley seems to have one.

buy.item: a string bag of retired netting

maker.d: Match spinballs stitched in twelve panels and weighed to the gram, because the league has a rule about weight and players argue about everything else. Schools on the row order them by the crate.

Spinning tops made for the third-g terraces, where the point carries a third of the weight and a good top spins for minutes. Children race them in chalk rings, and the champion top lives in a case at the school.

Kites of bamboo spills and dyed paper, light enough to rise on a walking child's pull. On the Hollow floor they need a run; on the top terraces a stroll will do, and the far bank always flies a few back.

Rope for the end-wall climbs, braided from vat fibre and dyed by rating: red for the heavy lower tiers, white for the top terraces, where a fall is mostly floating. Climbers here read a rope before they trust it.

Flying discs balanced to be thrown anti, where they lose a little weight and sail and sail. Thrown spinward they dive at your feet, and the shop's range is painted with both directions so you learn quickly.

Its sleeve-makers hardly make sleeves: they reline them in this year's colour, so a pair can go through four owners and look like nobody's. Leave old sleeves on a Thursday and fly in them by Saturday.

Hand lamps of a watt or two that clip to a wing-sleeve's cuff, made in a dozen colours for the Long Flight. The drum flies in its own colours, so from the end wall the axis looks like a river with a pattern in it.

buy.item: a cuff lamp for the Long Flight

maker.d: Half the herb shelves on the row grow under lamps from here, tuned so a metre of basil and shiso does well on a watt or two. The makers test each one on their own shelf, and the shop smells like a very cheap salad.

Paper shades dyed to turn a 200-lux room any colour you like, which costs nothing to run, since colour is free and brightness isn't. People here change their shades the way other drums change collars.

The 2,500-lux panels that schoolchildren sit beside for twenty minutes each morning are made here, framed in birch and remade when the frames crack. Running one costs about a hundredth of a kay a morning, and parents still mention it.

Night lamps that lay a faint band of gold, frayed with brown-violet, across a bedroom ceiling, for children who haven't been to the Window yet. Parents argue about whether it spoils the surprise, and buy one anyway.

Its lamp-painters sell scores: the colour and timing of a dawn, written so any drum's sunline can play it. Copies are free; a printed score with the painter's notes in the margin is not, and those are the ones people frame.

buy.item: a printed dawn score with the painter's notes

maker.d: Felt for rooms that ring, pressed from cellulose fibre in rolls as wide as a corridor. Every hall on the row hangs some, and the felters can tell which room they're in with their eyes shut.

Quilts pieced from tailors' offcuts, so they cost almost no new mass and a great many hours. Each comes with a list of where its pieces were before: a wedding dress, a back-crew lining, three school shirts.

Coats come in by the crate to be relined in this year's colour, which this year is a hard blue-green. The lining is a few hundred grams of spun cellulose; the craft is getting it in without the coat noticing.

buy.item: a coat relined in this year's colour

maker.d: A school of visible mending, where every darn is done in a colour that argues with the cloth. The masters' own coats are so mended that the first cloth is mostly a rumour.

buy.item: an elbow darned in gold thread

maker.d: Vats of colour where a grey shirt goes in and comes out this year's green for less than a cup of coffee in dye. Guests are invited to dip a hand, and walk round with it coloured for all three nights.

buy.item: a shirt re-dyed while you wait

maker.d: Collars that button on and off, so the whole drum can change its look for a festival without touching a coat. A family's collar drawer is usually older than its sofa.
Scarves woven from vat silk, the shimmering repeat-protein the Vats make by the gram, and painted by hand. One weighs about as much as a letter; most of the price is the painter's afternoon.

Shoes of mycelium leather, fitted by makers who ask which deck you live on before your size, because soles wear faster where you weigh more. Fittings are on {weekday}s, and most people resole for years while they wait.
Every inn leaves a basket outside each guest door, and by lamp-dawn the shoes inside are resoled and back. Wanderers arrive in boots that have walked half the raft and leave sounding new.

buy.item: a pair of shoes resoled overnight

maker.d: Children's clothes cut with a hand's width folded into every seam, so trousers can be let out three times before they're handed on. The cutters here claim the double fold, and will show you.

buy.item: a child's shirt with growing seams

maker.d: Thick robes for the baths, woven loose because cloth dries fast in heliox, and long because the walk from the water is the coldest part of anyone's day. Every block bath on the row has a rack of them.

Wedding clothes are the clothes you have, altered, and this drum's cutters are the best on the row at it: a grey dress turns green, a father's jacket fits his son. Couples come a month early and leave looking new.

buy.item: a jacket re-cut for a wedding

maker.d: Stitched patches of the River, pale gold with a frayed brown-violet edge, sewn for children the week they come back from the Window. The first is free; a second costs the stitcher's afternoon.

Its paper, pressed from Hollow bamboo pulp, is made for a long letter that will be read once, years from now, by someone who will keep it. The works make a few hundred sheets a day and stop when the pulp runs out.

Inks made to dry fast in heliox without clogging a nib, in colours named for drums along the row. The black is famous, and the brown-violet the back crews call bruise sells out before every Booking Day.

A type foundry whose letters are read all over Merrow, since copies cost nothing and good faces travel. The drum asks only that you say where they came from, and sells printed specimen sheets to people who like holding things.
Binders who sew a whole correspondence, both sides of a lifetime's long letters, into one book. A book is mass and nobody buys one lightly, so most families have one shelf, and it is mostly letters.

buy.item: your letters bound in birch boards

maker.d: Illustrators who draw the picture on the front of a card home while you watch. The card goes by light and weighs nothing; the drawing takes twenty minutes, and for most wanderers it's the dearest thing they buy that week.

buy.item: a card front drawn while you wait

maker.d: Hand-drawn maps of all 375 decks, redrawn whenever a block moves a wall. People buy the map of the deck they were born on and hang it in the kitchen.

buy.item: a printed map of one deck

maker.d: Slates for the wood drums' silences: birch frames, a face of remade stone, a stick of chalk on a string. Each is tested by writing a whole argument on it and wiping it clean.

buy.item: a slate and three sticks of chalk

maker.d: Pens with nibs ground from heirloom metal, so a grandmother's ring can become a grandson's handwriting. The grinders work in a room hung with felt on all six sides, where a dropped nib is the loudest thing all week.
Seals carved for namings, with the child's name on one face and the name of the dead whose share they carry on the other. Families stamp both on the note they send the dead's family each year.

Knives remade from returned steel, ground on wheels that have turned for three centuries. Cooks from every hall on the row send their blades here once a year, and {name} at the wheel knows each hall by its chips.
Every spoon here used to be something else, and is stamped to say so: fork, ladle, cake slice, once a door handle. Children collect the odd ones.
Clocks whose faces show the lamp clock: a pale arc for lamp-dawn, a long white band for the day, a dark stretch for the machines. The best of them dim their own faces at eleven.

A glaze school whose colours go on cups all over the row, mixed from grams of pigment, since colour weighs almost nothing. The famous one is a green that looks grey under home lamps and turns green in the Hollow.

buy.item: a glazed cup with a lid

maker.d: Lids made to fit the bowls you already own: leave a bowl overnight and it comes back covered. Food goes cold fast in heliox, and this drum has made a trade of making sure nobody's does.

buy.item: a lid made to fit a bowl you bring

maker.d: Stoneware crocks for larders, thick-walled and lidded, in sizes named for how long they'd feed a family in the Dark: a week, a fortnight, a month. Most kitchens on the row have at least one fortnight.

Glass blown on the end-wall terraces at a third of a g, where a gather sags slowly enough to be pulled thin and wide. The furnaces are electric and the glass is mostly old lift panes, which few drinkers know.

Heavy pans that hold their heat, because searing draws power and a pan with mass sears fast and then rests. Cooks inherit them; a new one costs two weeks of dinners and is only sold to someone who will use it.
Tiles for the baths, painted by hand and glazed to look warm through steam. Block baths all over the row have a wall from here, and children learn to swim lengths by counting the pictures.
Buttons cut from heirloom metal: an old clasp makes six, a broken spoon four. People bring what they can't bear to send back to the Yards, and wear it on their cuffs.

buy.item: six buttons from an old clasp

maker.d: Lidded teapots with felt cosies, built to hold heat in air that steals it. The potters swear a pot keeps tea hot an hour longer than any machine-made one, and nobody has ever timed it.
Four hundred sourdoughs live in its starter library, each registered with the strain library and fed by a rota of volunteers. Wanderers may take a spoon of any they like, and most take three.
Vinegar mothers in glass jars along the cooler pipes, some older than the drum's oldest chair. Each jar crosses the Gate with a tag, and the Gate crews call the queue for them the vinegar line.

buy.item: a jar of vinegar mother, tagged for the Gate

maker.d: Yogurt cultures from families all over the drum, kept in a warm room off the Quaysides and sequenced so nobody's grandmother's yogurt can take down a vat. Visitors taste a flight of nine on little spoons.

Cheese aged in rooms chilled to cellar cool, which costs real power in a drum that runs warm, so the cheesemakers share their cold with the strain library's store next door. They know each wheel by the sound it makes when tapped.

Koji grown on Mill rice in rooms kept at body heat, which costs nothing in a drum that runs warm anyway. The koji-makers sleep in shifts beside it, because a tray left an hour too long grows the wrong mould.
Miso aged three, five and ten years in larder crocks, and one crock started the year after the Eleven Days that nobody may open. A spoon of the ten-year is the usual gift to a new household.
Cell-culture tea blended with herbs cut on the terraces: one blend for lamp-dawn, one for the long dusk, one for the night before a glide. Each is named after a person, and nobody will say who.

buy.item: a tin of the dusk blend

maker.d: Five weeks on the 65 °C loop turns garlic soft, sweet and black, and costs nothing but patience. The ageing rooms smell of molasses, and the workers stopped noticing long ago.
Chilli crisp fried in small batches in the lamp-night, when power for frying is cheapest, and sold warm at lamp-dawn. Every family on the row claims a different jar is the real recipe.

A grafting school that supplies scions to block Courts across the row, so most espaliered pears within ten glides have a parent here. The graft-cutters keep a book of every tree, its children, and which ever gave a pear worth eating.

buy.item: a pear scion, registered for the Gate

maker.d: Rooted cuttings of basil, shiso and coriander from lines kept going for centuries, potted with a lid for the glide. The basil line called Old Hessa is the most-given host gift on the row.

buy.item: a rooted basil cutting in a pot

maker.d: Amazake brewed overnight at 60 °C on the waste-heat loop, sweet and thick, poured hot at the station rings at lamp-dawn. The brewers start it at one in the morning with the laundry, and by four the whole Keel smells of it.
Mushrooms grown on the Hollow's pruned birch and bamboo, in rooms that need no light at all, which makes them one of the few fresh foods that cost no lamps. Halls on the row buy them by the basket.
Shadow puppets of dyed paper, played against hall walls by hand lamp, since colour costs nothing and a shadow costs less. The great show runs one night a year and is never recorded, on purpose.
A board game invented here three centuries ago, played on a ring where pieces moving spinward grow heavier and slower, and nobody has ever settled a draw. Sets are turned from chair offcuts.

buy.item: a travelling set in a cloth roll

maker.d: Its dice-makers insist that grinding a die true in a room that turns is harder than it sounds, and nobody has proved them right or wrong. Dice are sold in pairs, and a pair is never split.
Paper masks for Knotnight, when the lamps go down and the larder is made: a face for the dark and a face for the morning, folded one inside the other. Children here wear them backwards for luck.
A store of festival costumes going back centuries, re-dyed every year so nobody wears the same colour twice. You hire one for the night and bring it back, and the price is mostly the dyer's hour.

buy.item: a costume, hired and re-dyed for you

maker.d: Wanderers sleep better on the weightless slow lines in its bags, which have a clip at each shoulder and a hood that keeps your hair out of your mouth. Riders who use one stop waking up sideways.
Bulb cups for soup at zero g and string nets for bread, made for the cycler galleys and anyone about to ride them. The kit comes in a pouch with a clip, because anything without a clip leaves.

buy.item: a bulb cup and a bread net

maker.d: Small sealed crocks with a strain-library tag already on, for carrying a spoon of starter through a year of Gates. Wanderers come home with them full of other people's sourdough and a tag from every drum.
Harnesses for the slow line's daily bungee hour, padded where the cords pull and adjustable for anyone from a twenty-year-old to an aunt. Wanderers buy them before the first leg and curse them after.

steady.d: Strawberries from lit racks in the Keel, sold at the Quaysides by the half-dozen and wrapped in paper like rings. Neighbours glide over on rest days and eat them on the platform before the glide home.

buy.item: six strawberries in a paper twist

steady.d: Twenty-two hens on vat feed behind a glass wall on deck {deck}, and a waiting list for their eggs that runs past the next Booking Day. Parents bring children to watch one cracked: a whole gold yolk, sitting up in the bowl.

Two hundred and fourteen chairs on deck {hdeck}, each labelled with its owners and its mends. The oldest has had eleven seats and four sets of legs, and a vote every ten years confirms it is still the same chair.
The best ring-counter broth on {row}, in the opinion of everyone on {row} except the five nearest drums. It is held for two days on the 65 °C loop and has never once been allowed to boil.

The longest strain library on its row: nine thousand starters, yogurts, vinegar mothers and koji lines, each an heirloom and a file. The librarians will tell you which family's crock saved the bread line after the last blight, and then tell you again.

Its Gate at Station Ring {ring} caught a dormant phage in a crock of pickled radish a week before the pickles would have reached the dairy vats. The crew get a cake on the date every year, and the crock is still in the isolation vault.
Baths on the 65 °C loop with eleven pools in a row, each a degree warmer than the last, so you work your way up like a slow stair. The last pool is for elders and the very brave.

On the anniversary of its worst protein-flour blight, every hall serves the Nine as a salty paste on starch toast, and people who were children then go quiet over it. The young ask for it all year, which annoys their grandparents enormously.
A cucumber house on the end-wall terraces, lit mostly by the Hollow's own glow, with a little lamp to finish. Cucumbers are sold cold and cut thick, and a whole one is a proper engagement present.

buy.item: a cold cucumber, cut thick and salted

steady.d: Every school class gets one morning a year in the radish beds on the Hollow floor, and each child pulls and eats one radish, soil and all. Nobody likes radishes at eight. Everybody remembers them.
Three tiers of low-chill apples on the front end wall, where the light is gentlest. The fruit goes by lottery, and winners frame the ticket long after the apple has been cut, shared and eaten.

Cherry tomatoes grown in racks along the Hollow's edge and sent in sealed crates to the Gates of half its row. The crate labels are hand-lettered by one family, who have lettered them for ninety years.

buy.item: a paper cone of cherry tomatoes

steady.d: A fig trained flat against the brightest wall of a Court on deck {deck}, a hundred and sixty years old and good for about forty figs a year. They go one each to the block's newlyweds, which is why weddings there are timed to the figs.
One lemon tree grows in a pot in a lift lobby, under a lamp the whole block pays for. Its zest goes by a waiting list eleven years long, and people leave their place on the list in their wills.

Six generations of one family have run the mending shop on {street}, and they keep a book of every coat they have relined. Bring in your grandmother's coat and they can tell you the colour of its first lining.

buy.item: a coat relined in this year's colour

steady.d: Four hundred block teams play spinball in the long halls of the Low decks, near full weight. The final is held at a third of a g on the end-wall terraces, where every throw breaks wildly and everyone claims they meant it.

For three centuries a Low-deck school has taught arithmetic with dropped cups: every child measures how far antispinward a cup lands and works out why. The school has broken about forty thousand cups and had every one remade.

Its Windows look out on the largest raft shape anyone on its row can see, a black disc about a fingernail wide at arm's length. Children come back from their eighth-year visit able to draw it exactly, and many keep drawing it for years.

A Window guide, {name}, who has taken more than forty thousand eight-year-olds out to see the River and has never let a group skip the twenty minutes in the red light. People who went with {name} as children ask for the same guide for their own.

Its back crews keep a spare suit in every size and will take a visitor for half a shift behind the radiators, if they sign for the dose and hold the tools. Most come back quiet and buy the crew a drink.

A gin cellar under the Quaysides that steeps each week's gin with herbs travellers leave on the counter, written up in a book by the till. It sells near cost with thiamine in it, and the herb of the week is chalked up with the name of whoever left it.

buy.item: a glass of this week's gin

steady.d: Vat cheeses age up to six years on bamboo shelves in a cold room cut into the Keel beside the water works. The cave master tastes every wheel once a month and tells each one what she thinks of it.

buy.item: a wedge of six-year cave cheese

steady.d: Every {weekday} two hundred stalls on the Quaysides sell what the drum's larders can spare: radish, cucumber, black beans, sugared plums, things nobody can name. Everything is tasted off a bamboo pick and judged out loud.

buy.item: a jar of three-year radish pickle

steady.d: Its mycelium steaks from the year after the long blight are reckoned the best vintage on its row, and the strain library keeps that exact line on ice. Halls across the row grow it again for anniversaries and pretend not to compare.

The bakery on deck {deck} registered its starter with the strain library 412 years ago, and its bakers still get up at three to feed it. The queue for the morning loaf goes round the corner and up a stair.

One block has kept a basil line alive on its herb shelves for six hundred years, cutting by cutting, never once grown back from the library. Every child in the block is given a cutting at their naming, and most keep it going.
A small museum of the Eleven Days, kept by the last people who remember them, with a dark room you can stand in for eleven minutes. Children go in laughing and come out holding hands.

A water clock six decks tall in the atrium of the oldest block, whose drops land a little antispinward as every falling thing here must. It has been reset twice in three centuries, and the keeper's notes on why are framed beside it.

The inside of Lift Core {n} is painted from the Keel to the Hollow, so a cab ride passes the drum's whole history in about ninety seconds. Children ride it up and down on purpose, and nobody stops them.
A bay tree in the Court of the oldest block, older than any family in it, whose leaves flavour every stew within three corridors. Taking a leaf without asking is the block's one real crime.

An arcade on deck {deck} that runs right round the drum and comes back to where it started, a long afternoon's walk. Walk it spinward and you are a little heavier the whole way round, which locals say builds character.
Forty benches along the back shore of the Hollow lake, each named for the elder who sat on it longest. A new elder is given a bench when one falls vacant, and nobody discusses how.

A soup bar inside the netting of the front flying hall, serving soup in squeeze bulbs and bread in string bags. Regulars drift in wearing wing-sleeves, eat hanging from a strap, and leave crumbs that take ten minutes to settle.

buy.item: a bulb of soup and a roll in a net

steady.d: On Knotnight the whole of {street} turns into a larder fair, each block laying out its best preserves for the others to taste and swap. The judges are children, who always choose the sweetest thing.

On Booking Day one cloth is laid down the Hollow floor from end wall to end wall, three and three-quarter kilometres of it, and seats along it go by lottery. It is two hundred years old and mended in every colour the drum has ever liked.
Once a year every block shows the smallest object it owns that is still in use. Last year's winner was a thimble with nine owners' initials scratched inside it, the first of them too worn to read.

Someone has rung the bell on the top terrace of the front end wall by hand at the start of every lamp-dawn for four hundred years. It rings high and clear in heliox, and about five seconds later the far bank hears it, faintly, like an answer.

A coat library on deck {deck}: two thousand good coats with their owners' mends, lent for a festival or an interview and returned with one small mend of your own. The busiest coat has been out four hundred times and fits nobody well.

In the old Quaysides arcade, the Hollow-hours exchange lets people swap their deck's turns, trade lamp-dawn hours for lamp-night ones, and buy hours as gifts. A bell rings whenever an hour changes hands for a wedding.

Once a year the drum judges its longest-kept starter, on the strain library's dates and a slice of bread from each. The same crock has won for nineteen years, and its family carries it in under a padded lid like a sleeping baby.

The week before Knotnight, a Mill Hall gives a prize for the best herb shelf under thirty centimetres long. The winning shelf feeds its owner's stews for a year and its owner's pride for a good deal longer.
A yearly prize for a repair nobody can find. The judges search each coat for an hour with lamps and lenses, and the winner is whichever coat they give up on.

buy.item: an invisible darn on a sleeve or knee

steady.d: A cab line that runs in a glass channel along the side of the biggest Court in the drum, so for eleven seconds you ride past a six-deck wall of espaliered pears. People take it on the way to somewhere else, on purpose.

A long letter that crossed eight light-years of the Shade from a child on another raft, read aloud in the same hall every year since it landed. The drum wrote back that week, so an answer to the answer is due any year now.

Some eight thousand steps climb the whole height of the drum, Keel to Hollow, and once a year a few thousand people with packed lunches climb them. You start at a full g and finish at half, and halfway up everyone agrees it was a terrible idea.

It has sat at par, give or take a few thousand people, for six hundred years. The figure is painted by hand over the arch at Station Ring {ring}, and the painter has never had to change more than the last three digits.
Everyone sees the Window once at eight and, if they ask, again at ninety. The ninety-year-olds' sittings are the quietest room in the drum, and the guides say the questions are the same ones.
Every {weekday}, forty orchard apples are drawn among everyone who planted, pruned or picked in the Hollow's orchards that week. Winners are expected to cut theirs crosswise in public and share it.

A lamp shop on {street} that has made hand lamps for the Long Flight for three hundred years, each shade dyed to order. On Booking night you can pick its lamps out from the Hollow floor: they are the slightly greener ones.

buy.item: a hand lamp with a dyed shade

steady.d: A grapevine trained along the ceiling of a whole arcade on deck {deck}, under a strip of grow lamps the arcade's shops pay for between them. It gives a few kilos of small sour grapes a year, which the arcade pickles and serves on toast at namings.
Lamp-dawn swimming in the Hollow lake for anyone over ninety, with towels warmed on the 65 °C loop and a cup of broth on the steps. At half a g, ninety-year-olds dive, and some of them show off.
Its ring counters put a pickled plum in the middle of the free rice ball, a habit started by one counter hand two centuries ago and copied, grudgingly, by all nine rings.
For three hundred years a noodle shop on the Low decks has served the same bowl: glass noodles in black vinegar with chilli crisp and too much garlic. Families bring new babies in just to smell it.

buy.item: a bowl of the same noodles

steady.d: A chilli crisp made in one block's kitchens since before the Eleven Days, crunchy with puffed starch and dark with Mill sesame. Jars leave in travellers' bags for half the raft, and the block will not say what the brown bits are.

buy.item: a jar of the block's chilli crisp

steady.d: Black garlic aged five weeks on the 65 °C loop in racks under the Keel, soft and sweet as fruit. Gate crews from drums three glides away come in to buy it, which is high praise from people who see everything.
Custards of vat egg held at 63 °C for an hour in the baths' own pipes, sold at the baths' door. You eat one in a robe, with a spoon that lives in a jar of hot water.

buy.item: an onsen custard in its cup

steady.d: Amazake brewed overnight in the Keel's waste heat and carried up to the lift lobbies in lidded urns before lamp-dawn. Crews coming off the lamp-night drink it standing up and say it tastes like going home.

The best jook on its row, by long agreement, made in the Mill Hall nearest Station Ring {ring} from a stock that never boils. The cook adds the chilli crisp herself and will not discuss the ratio with anyone.

A squash vine that has climbed four tiers of the back end wall, pruned by a terrace committee with very strong views. At a third of a g its fruit grow enormous without tearing loose, and the biggest goes into the Booking Day soup.

{name} has cooked the same Knotnight pie in the same hall for sixty years. The crust recipe has been copied ten million times and is only flour, fat and water, and nobody else has ever made it come out like that.

A darning circle that meets in the warm room behind the baths every {weekday} and has darned the same families' socks for five generations. A pair of its socks is a traditional wedding present, which is either sweet or a warning.

A cobbler's on the Quaysides that resoles shoes while you wait, in mycelium leather grown two decks down. Travellers time their glides around it and sit in their socks on a bench that has held three centuries of people in socks.
A barber on deck {deck} who has cut hair in the same chair for seventy years and charges a full hour for twenty minutes, on the grounds that you will be talking for the other forty.

On the Low decks a child can borrow a top, a kite or a weighted ball from the toy library, and must bring it back with a story of something it did. The stories are kept, and there are more than a million.

Its dark Mill lager is brewed in the Keel to a recipe older than anyone can prove and sold in every hall at the cost of the sugar. Travellers ask for it by name on other drums and are given whatever is on tap.
Every station ring sells the same tea: a third jasmine, a third roast, a third whatever the Hollow's herb beds gave that week. It is never the same twice, and people complain when it is.

Down in the Keel, a public room is kept at twelve degrees, and people go there to wear their good coats. It is the only place in the drum where a scarf is not a joke, and teenagers go there to look serious.

The glide cars at Station Ring {ring} have the widest aft windows on its row, through a full metre of clear water. People ride out to the next drum and straight back, two minutes and twenty seconds each way, just to look.

Its quay lights are amber, not white, by a vote taken three hundred years ago, so from any glide window on the row you can pick out {drum}'s ring among the ranks. Children on the drums around call it the warm one.

A great dial in the Mill Hall on deck {deck} that shows not hours but lamp-dawn, lamp-noon and lamp-night, with a small extra hand for the laundry. People set their days by the big hands and their washing by the small one.

Soap made in the Keel from Mill fats and scented from the flavourist's rack with a smell the drum votes on each year: pear, cut grass, warm bread. Old people can date a memory by how their hands smelled.

buy.item: a cake of this year's soap

steady.d: The Gate's isolation vault keeps visiting hours, so anyone can come and sit with a culture they weren't allowed to bring in. On a rest day the bench is full of people talking quietly to jars.
Its blue cheese owes its mould to a traveller's sleeve: caught at the Gate two hundred years ago, sequenced, found harmless and kept because it tasted so good. The traveller's name is on every label.
A shop on {street} that sells single tomatoes in lined boxes, priced in the window like rings. More proposals are made with them than anyone will admit to.

An archive of recordings from the old air, every voice sounding as if spoken through a blanket, where people go to hear how their ancestors might have sounded. Most come out speaking softly for an hour.
Seven layers of felt line its best concert room, the quietest on its row, so a string quartet can play softer there than anywhere else in the drum. Tickets are cheap, and the coughs are famous.

A wedding terrace on the back end wall at a third of a g, where a couple leaps together once and lands a hand's width spinward, which is said to mean a good start. Booking it takes a year and both families' Hollow hours.
A mushroom cellar in the Keel growing shiitake on spent bamboo from the Hollow, sold in paper bags at the Quaysides at lamp-dawn. The growers smell faintly of it and are proud of that too.
Dumplings folded with exactly eighteen pleats. The seventeen school and the nineteen school have argued with the eighteen school for two centuries, from neighbouring counters, without once speaking.
Eight hundred elders rehearse their choir in the lift lobby of deck {hdeck}, because it rings best. The deck's residents gave up complaining years ago and joined.
At the end of the bath row is a cold plunge so cold in heliox that hardly anyone stays in for a count of ten. The names of those who have are on a board by the steps, and the board is short.

A red stew served from one pot in the Mill Hall by Station Ring {ring}, topped up daily and never emptied, which its cooks call the eighty-year stew. They admit, if pressed, that this is a figure of speech.
A long bed of four-o'clock flowers on the Hollow floor that open all at once as the sunline's dusk begins. It takes about a minute, and people plan proposals around it.

Every year the Low-deck schools paint a new mural over last year's on the corridor outside, so the walls there are three centuries thick. A chipped corner shows every colour the drum has ever liked, in order.

The best Gate school on its row, where trainees learn to spot a prophage in a sequence and a smuggled crock in a traveller's face. Its graduates work Gates across half the raft and send cards home about what they caught.
Dawn knots, twists of laminated pastry, are baked at five and sold until the sunline reaches full. Whatever is left after nine is given away, which is why the drum's children are all early risers.
A herb market on {street} at every lamp-dawn: two hundred stalls of cuttings, nothing over a tenth of a kWh, and haggling anyway. Host gifts for the whole row are bought here.

buy.item: a bunch of mixed cuttings for a host

steady.d: A table in the Mill Hall on deck {deck} that has seated every newly married couple in the block for four centuries, made from one plank of Hollow yew. It has been planed so many times that it is now thinner than a door.

Its blocks vote every year on whether to light the Court bright or the terraces evenly, and the Court has won ninety-one years running. The terrace flats have a club, a newsletter and very good lamps.
It has more people over a hundred and ten than any drum on its row, which it puts down to its stairs and its neighbours put down to its gin.

Its sunline has run two minutes behind the raft's clock for nine hundred years, after an argument nobody can now explain. Its people are famously and cheerfully late everywhere else, and say they are the only ones on time.

Every front door in the drum is painted the same blue, by a vote taken three hundred years ago and never repealed. Visitors are lost at once; residents find their way by the handles, which are all different.

On the Quaysides, the perfumers' counter will mix any flavour molecule you can name to the part per million, from saffron to the smell of old paper. The perfumers who run it can tell your block from your hair oil.

buy.item: a twist of the house spice blend

steady.d: A pear orchard on the Hollow floor where every school class pollinates one tree with brushes and later gets a share of its pears. Children argue for years about whose tree is best, and the trees outlast the arguments.
The laundry runs at one in the morning, as everywhere, but here a co-op of night workers folds it all by hand. A shirt folded in {drum} is recognised on any platform on its row.
Three thousand lids, from a bamboo cap for a tea cup to a dome for a whole roast, in a museum whose keeper says you can read a drum's history in what it chose to keep warm.
A dark loaf baked only on {weekday}s, from a starter that the bakers swear refuses to rise on any other day. The queue starts at four, and regulars bring stools.

A herb garden climbing nine tiers of the front end wall, one kitchen herb to a tier, ending in a mint terrace near the axis where mint grows like a weed at almost no weight. Cooks send apprentices up for it as a test of legs.
