Every eight-year-old learns to swim in the Hollow lake the week after their Window, a pairing nobody remembers choosing. Teachers swear that children who have just seen the River are fearless in water.
One Keel workshop has ground the same mustard since before anyone kept count, sharp enough to make a grown cook sit down. A pot goes home with every guest who has been rude about it.
Its air-handling fans were tuned two centuries ago to hum one low chord together, and people who move away say they cannot sleep anywhere else. Visitors notice it on the first night and never again.

A map of every drum within a hundred glides, painted on the concourse wall at Station Ring {ring} and corrected in pencil by travellers. Some corrections have been corrected, and some of those are rude.
A tailor on deck {deck} who changes nothing but collars, and has set the row's fashion three years in five. Her window is watched closely from three drums away.

buy.item: a new collar on an old shirt

steady.d: Half the drum re-dyes its coats at one dye works the week before Booking Day, so the arcades change colour in a few days. The colour costs nearly nothing; the queue is the expensive part.

buy.item: a coat re-dyed in this year's colour

steady.d: A desk in the registry that helps families write the yearly note to the family of the person whose share their child carries. It keeps drafts going back four centuries, and some families copy a great-grandmother's word for word.
Four thousand paper books fill a reading room, the heaviest library on its row, kept because some things ought to weigh something. You may read anything there and borrow nothing.
A bakery that gives a free bun to anyone who brings in something they have mended that week, to be shown, admired and taken home again. On a good day the counter looks like a repair shop.

buy.item: a bun, for anyone without a mend

steady.d: From the ten-metre tower by the Hollow lake, a dive at half a g takes long enough to change your mind twice. Children count it out loud from the bank.

A writing room on deck {hdeck}, lit warm and kept silent, with desks booked by the week for anyone writing a long letter. The rule is to leave it as quiet as you found it, and people take the rule personally.
A hot pot hall where forty tables share one broth piped up from the 65 °C loop, and each table brings its own pot to the boil. Most of the bill is keeping it there.

buy.item: a seat at the hot pot

steady.d: One fry shop prices by the minute of frying rather than by the food, because searing draws power and the loop cooks everything else free. The menu board is a clock.

buy.item: a paper cone of fried jelly cubes

steady.d: A puppet theatre on the Low decks that has played the same show about the Eleven Days for seventy years, with the lamps going down in the middle. Children who have seen it twenty times still shout when the Glide brings food.

buy.item: a seat at the puppet show

steady.d: Ninety flavours of lokum on a Mill-sugar base, all dusted in starch. Rose is the one everyone buys, and pistachio, made with real nuts from the Garden, is the one people point at.

The lift lobby on deck {hdeck} has a moss wall three decks tall, kept green by the lobby's own lamps and the breath of everyone waiting. People let a cab go by to stand in front of it a little longer.
Its school lunches are cooked by retired hall cooks, paid in Hollow hours and complaints. Children from neighbouring drums try to transfer for the dumplings.

Its vats run a few degrees warm, so the hot tap gives seventy instead of sixty-five and its tea is made a little faster than anyone's. Its people are known everywhere else for being impatient with kettles.

buy.item: a pot of tea from the hot tap

steady.d: A Spindle lift with a glass cabin up the back end wall, the slowest on its row on purpose, so riders can watch the floor fall away and feel their weight leave them a little at a time. Elders ride it to the top and straight back down.
On the arrivals platform at Station Ring {ring}, elders who won't glide any more sit on a row of benches and watch the cars come in. They know half the row by sight and the other half by luggage.
Its ring counters wrap the free rice ball in paper printed with a two-line poem, new each week, by whoever won the drum's poem lottery. Travellers keep them in their coat linings.
A whispering gallery in the dome over the oldest Court, where a word said at one wall arrives clear at the other, forty metres off. Couples test it, and elders use it for gossip.

thin.d: Inns near the station rings let each bunk three times a day in eight-hour shifts, with clean sheets between sleepers and a crew that takes pride in it. Travellers swear they're the best-made beds on the row.

Most rooms here have three lives a day: a schoolroom until two, a workshop until eight, a dormitory until morning. The furniture folds into the walls, and any class can turn its room into beds for forty in under five minutes.

Power is cheapest in the lamp-night, so the stalls on {street} cook from midnight to lamp-dawn, when frying costs least. The best fried dough on the row comes out at three in the morning, and so does half the block.

buy.item: a twist of fried dough at three in the morning

thin.d: Every Mill Hall serves dinner in four sittings, half an hour apart, and the tables are cleared and laid again to a bell. Regulars know their sitting like a birthday, and changing it takes a vote of the whole table.

The busiest swaps desk on the row sits by Station Ring {ring}: families trading flats up and down the decks, lodgers after a corner, couples trying to live on the same deck at last. The clerks know half the drum's floor plans by heart.
A choir of six hundred that can never fit in one room, so it rehearses in three shifts and only sings together on Booking Day, in the Hollow. Every part has three leaders who have never met.
The best food on the row for under a kWh: jook with three toppings, glass-noodle salad, fried jelly cubes in black vinegar. Cooks from roomier drums glide in on their days off to see how it's done.

buy.item: a bowl of jook with three toppings

thin.d: A whole deck of stalls where nothing is new and everything was once something else: coats cut from bigger coats, a chair built from three, a lampshade that used to be a colander. Buyers come from three glides away for the honest prices and the mending.

buy.item: a coat cut down from a bigger one

thin.d: Baths that never close, because somebody is always coming off a shift. The water runs off the food plant's loop and costs almost nothing, and at four in the morning the steam room is full of bakers and back crews talking quietly.

With so many people and so little Hollow, the drum keeps its floor open all through the lamp-night, and the night turns are the ones families fight to keep. They picnic by hand lamp under the dark far bank while the children sleep on the grass.
Every corner of {block} has a café where you bring something broken and somebody at the next table fixes it. The fixing is free; buying them a tea is how you pay.

buy.item: a tea for whoever fixed your thing

thin.d: A tailor on {street} who lets out, takes in or turns any garment in under an hour while you sit in a borrowed robe. Children's trousers here are let out four times, not three, and she has opinions about the fourth.

buy.item: trousers let out while you wait

thin.d: The schools teach two shifts a day, early and late, and the children of each shift leave notes in the desks for the other. Some pairs write for years before they meet, and a few of them marry.

Card games run in every lift lobby on fold-down tables, played by people waiting for a cab, a bunk or a sitting. The local game takes about four minutes a hand, which is how long anything here makes you wait.

There's no hall to spare, so plays go up in corridors and lift lobbies, with the audience on the stairs. The actors learn to carry a line in heliox without shrieking, and several of the row's best started here.

Flats here are too small for a herb shelf each, so every stairwell has a tall lit column of herbs shared by the floors it passes, with a rota pinned at the bottom. Its basil is the best on the row, and its rota the longest.

Nobody rides a cab alone if they can help it: you hold the door at the berth, call your deck, and anyone going your way gets in. Strangers have met this way for so long that a fair share of the drum's marriages began between decks.

Every residential corridor has a bench every twenty metres, because the flats are too small to sit guests in. In the evenings the corridors are the living rooms, and their ceiling felt is the best-kept on the row.

Shareless adults who live on their families' wallets and lodge where they work have a club with its own hall, its own songs and a waiting list. Members call each other 'cousin' and turn up in a body at each other's weddings.

The drum is famous for its manners in a crowd: everyone steps antispinward to let a stretcher or a pram by, and lift queues form without a word. Visitors from emptier drums find it eerie, then miss it.

A noodle counter at Station Ring {ring} that has served the same broth for three hundred years, with fourteen stools and room for forty standing. The cook can pull, cut and serve a bowl in forty seconds and has never once been seen sitting down.

Most flats share a kitchen with three others, and the kitchens have become the drum's real parlours: a rota on the wall, four herb pots and one big lidded pot that is never quite empty. Visitors are fed from it whether they ask or not.

Its furniture makers build for small rooms: tables that fold flat, beds that become benches, a chair that hangs on a hook. Roomier drums copy the designs for free and still glide over to buy the hinges.

thin.t: The Court by the half hour
thin.d: Each block's Court light is shared by the half hour, every family taking its turn under the bright wall with a book or a baby. One family has kept the rota for six generations, and nobody has ever complained about it out loud.

Third children are less rare here than elsewhere, and their families meet once a month in one hall to trade outgrown clothes, cots and advice. Some hand-me-downs have a dozen names stitched inside the collar.
Laundries run all night when power is cheapest, and the folding tables at one in the morning are where the drum's news goes round. People bring a single shirt just to hear it.

buy.item: one shirt washed at one in the morning

thin.d: A dumpling shop whose queue runs down two decks of stairs, served by eleven cooks folding in a row. The queue has its own rules, its own jokes and a man who sells tea to it.

buy.item: six dumplings in a paper cone

thin.d: Each block pools its share of park light into one room lit like an overcast day, and its people take turns there by the hour: reading, sewing, sleeping off a night shift. It's the brightest room for three glides, and nobody owns it.

Wallets are thin and hours cheap, so most lift lobbies have live music in the evenings for about two kWh a night, split among whoever's waiting. Several well-known players started here and still come back to play the four-minute pieces the lobbies like.

Nothing is thrown away that can be cut down, turned or patched, and patches are worn proudly, in colours chosen to clash. A coat with five owners' mends is called 'well-housed', which is a compliment.

With no hall free, weddings are held in the corridors, guests lining both walls for a hundred metres. The apple is cut crosswise at one end and passed down the line, and by the far end it's in two hundred slivers and everyone has seen the star.

Flats are too small for a larder cupboard, so every flat keeps its larder under a floor hatch, and Knotnight here means the whole block on its knees at once. The pickles are the best on the row, possibly because they're kept so dark.

A shop where you borrow instead of buy: a ladder, a stockpot, a wedding coat, a second chair for when your aunt visits. Most of what's on its shelves is older than the drum's oldest resident, and the borrowers' book goes back three centuries.

buy.item: a wedding coat, borrowed for a day

thin.d: Spinball here is played in corridors, not halls, and the walls make every throw a bank shot. Its players are wanted by every team on the row for how well they read an angle.
Classes in everything from flute to accounts run through the lamp-night for people who work by day, in rooms that are bedrooms by morning. The night flute class is famous for playing very quietly.

The flats are famously small and famously clever: a bed over the door, a stair whose every step is a drawer, every wall a cupboard. Designers from roomier drums come to measure them and leave with notebooks full of drawings.
Nobody throws a cheaper festival than this drum, or a better one: Knotnight in the corridors, a lamp-night parade of a hundred thousand hand lamps, a Booking Day feast of jook with everything in it.

A board in the main concourse lists every family waiting for a bigger flat and how long they've waited, updated each night. When a family reaches the top, people they've never met leave herbs at their door.

Waste-heat cooking is a point of honour: whole dinners are held on the 65 °C loop for hours and nothing is fried that could be steamed, which keeps food bills the lowest on the row. Its onsen custards are famous; its fried things are not.

buy.item: an onsen custard in a lidded cup

thin.d: Once a week the long arcade closes to trolleys and becomes one table, each flat bringing a lidded dish. It runs three hundred metres, and the dishes travel up and down it all evening like slow trains.

counted.d: The Count at Station Ring {ring} is the oldest board in the drum, two numbers in plain white letters, people and places, and its keepers polish it every morning. When the gap closes by another hundred thousand, someone always brings them cake.
The whole drum bets on the day the Count will reach par, and the book is kept at a bakery on the Quaysides. Losers each owe the winner one tomato, and the last winner threw a salad for four thousand.

At fourteen every child here goes to the clinic for the fitting, and the evening after is a family dinner as big as a naming, with the child at the head of the table for the first time. Most people remember the dinner far better than the clinic.

The licence lottery is drawn in public once a month in the registry hall, the names read out by a different elder each time. Every winning couple stands, and the room claps for each one, the couples still waiting loudest of all.

Half the Low-deck classrooms have stood empty since the stop, and the drum has filled them with things that don't need children: a pottery, a seed bank, an orchestra's rehearsal rooms. The orchestra will have to move out in a few years, and is already sulking.

buy.item: a lidded bowl from the classroom pottery

counted.d: A hall of cooks under twenty-five who cook only from the Mill, a habit from the stop's early blight years, and win prizes for it across the row. Every dish costs under half a kWh, and the queue usually holds a chef or two from other rows, taking notes.

A big clock in the main concourse shows the days left to par, reset every Booking Day from the year's births and deaths. Children born once it dropped under a thousand are called 'clock children', and never let anyone forget it.

Last Booking Day the drum took down its Count board after {years} years and hung a Ledger in its place, with the old board kept beside it. People still stop in front of the pair on the way to the glide, and some of them touch the old one, as if to make sure it's really off the wall.

The drum's playgrounds, idle since the stop, have been planted as gardens by the elders who used to watch children in them. They're to be dug back into playgrounds the year births come back, and there's already a waiting list to do the digging.

buy.item: a herb cutting from the playground gardens

counted.d: With fewer children to raise, the drum has put its hours into its old: every elder on the high decks has a named visitor three times a week, and the clinics are the best-staffed on the row. Elders from neighbouring drums sometimes swap in on purpose.

The children's choir has eleven voices this year, the fewest in its history, and the whole drum turns out for every concert. The eleven are treated like a famous band and are mostly unbearable about it.

The swaps desk at Ring {ring} is the busiest in the metro: couples who want a child soon swapping out to drums with room, the childfree swapping in for the quiet streets. The clerks keep a box of tissues and a bowl of sweets on the counter, and need both.

A museum of every Count board from every stop in the drum's history, eleven of them, the oldest lettered by hand. Beside each is the date it came down and the first names given after, which is the part people read.

buy.item: a printed card of the oldest board

counted.d: Once a year the registry reads out the names of the dead whose shares went to licensed children, and the families on both sides meet for tea. Some pairs of families have kept meeting long after the children grew up.

On Booking Day the drum's oldest resident reads the Count aloud from the platform at Station Ring 1: people, places and the gap between. The gap gets a cheer whenever it shrinks, and this year the cheer went on for a long time.

The clothes bank has kept every outgrown child's coat and shoe from before the stop, mended, folded and waiting. When births pick up, the first children will be dressed entirely in heirlooms, and the volunteers have named every drawer.

The few children born each year grow up as one well-known year-group, called by the date of their parents' licence draw, and they stay close for life. 'Same draw' means more here than 'same school' anywhere else on the row.

The drum is already saving for its par feast, a few kays a year from every wallet into a fund kept at the Quaysides, and the menu is argued over weekly. Current favourites are cultivated steak for everyone and an apple for every two, cut crosswise.
At the fitting dinner a fourteen-year-old here gets their first good knife, an heirloom from an older relative, with their name added to the handle beside the others. Some knives carry six names.

The Low-deck arcades are quiet at four in the afternoon, when anywhere else they'd be full of children going home, so the drum has lined them with reading chairs and chess tables. The old play there in the hours that used to be the children's.

{name}, the nurse at the fitting clinic on deck {deck}, has fitted forty thousand fourteen-year-olds and remembers which ones cried. When they come back as adults to have the implant out on licence, they ask for {name} by name.

A small bell in the main concourse rings once for every licensed birth, about once a minute, and most days nobody hears it. When it fell silent for an afternoon during a repair, half the drum came down to ask what was wrong.

buy.item: a hand bell cast like the concourse bell

counted.d: With fewer children to raise, households here have more hours and kays to spare, and it shows in small ways: an apple at an ordinary birthday, a hall dinner on a Tuesday, linings in this year's blue.
With so few children, each one gets a crowd of godparents, and a Low-deck birthday here has about five adults for every child. The children are spoiled and cheerfully know it.

The drum is a few years from par, and the argument of the decade is whether to run the stop a little past it and keep the difference as a Margin, the way the open drums did. Both sides hold weekly suppers, and most people go to both for the food.

Every Booking Day a party of councillors glides to the nearest open drum to watch its Ledger read and comes home with notes. The notes are published, and read more widely than anything the council writes itself.

The stop began in a blight year, and on its anniversary the whole drum eats that year's menu: fried crunch instead of steak, starch custard, the Nine back on every table. Children who never saw the blight complain about it with great authority.

buy.item: a plate of the anniversary menu

counted.d: With fewer children to wear them out, the drum's toys last for ages, and the toy library on deck {deck} lends spinballs and kites three hundred years old. Children from the neighbouring drums glide over to borrow them.

Teachers outnumber pupils on some Low decks now, so lessons are nearly private, and the drum's twelve-year-olds take the row's mathematics prizes most years. The neighbours call it unfair and send their own children over for tutoring.

When {name} and Ivo drew a licence in the first lottery after the stop eased, they married in the main concourse under the Count board, hung with herb garlands for the day. Every couple since has tried to outdo it, and none has.

buy.item: a herb garland in the old style

counted.d: The drum has a whole book of songs from its birth stops, sung at fittings, licence draws and the day the Count comes down, and some are very funny. The best known is about a clerk who counted himself twice.

Newcomers who swap in, mostly people who don't want children, are met at the ring by a volunteer from their new block with a herb pot and a map. It's the best welcome on the row, and the drum knows exactly why it needs one.
Every lift lobby shows the Count in small numbers beside the deck number, so people here check the gap the way others check the time. Most can tell you it to the nearest thousand.

During the stop the drum gives its few young families extra Hollow hours, a whole morning a week, so the lake at lamp-dawn is full of babies bobbing at half a g. Elders who gave up their turns sit on the bank and watch, which they say is the better deal.
A single lamp in the main concourse has been kept dark since the stop began, to be lit the day the Count reads par. Children who never saw it lit argue about what colour it will be.

customs.t: On the avenues a cyclist riding spinward gives way to one riding anti, because the anti rider is lighter in the saddle and slower to stop.
Lost-property shelves stand on the antispinward side of every hall. It began as a joke about where dropped things go, and now it's simply where you look.
Children can tell whether a cab is going up or down with their eyes shut, from the way the cabin leans, and they test each other on every ride.
Dancers on the third-g terraces start each leap a hand's width antispinward of their mark, so the drum carries them home.
At weddings the couple throws a twist of herbs antispinward, where it sails over everyone's heads. Throwing it spinward, where it dives, means they've already picked who catches it.
Toasts are drunk 'up', toward the Hollow and the elders. Only Keel crews drink 'down', to the plant that feeds everyone, and they mean it.
Weights are always given 'at the rim', since every scale reads lighter the higher you live, and anyone quoting their high-deck weight is fooling nobody.
Tea is poured from no higher than a hand above the cup. Pour from any higher and the drum takes its share, a little antispinward of the cup.
A spinball game opens with one throw straight along the axis, the only fair direction, before anyone is allowed to throw anti.
A race that counts is run along the axis, where nobody gets heavier or lighter. Races run spinward or anti are for birthdays and for settling things.
When someone moves up to a high deck, friends carry the heaviest thing last, so they can feel it get lighter on the way.
A toddler's first visit to the Hollow is spent barefoot on the grass, falling over as often as they like, since at half a g it hardly hurts.
Grandchildren are allowed to run in the high-deck corridors, where a fall carries about half the bump it would at the rim, and the elders like the noise.
Parents on the upper decks take their children down to a Low deck to run for an hour most days, because bones grow best near full weight, or so every parent believes.
An old pendulum clock only keeps time on the deck it was made for, so when a family moves up, the eldest child goes with the clockmaker to have the pendulum shortened.
On the top terraces children try to jump the height of a house, and the best mark is chalked on the terrace wall until the next class comes up.
Kites are flown by running, since nothing else will lift them, so a kite day on the terraces is mostly a race in which nobody looks where they're going.
In the flying halls, whoever is flying along the axis has right of way over anyone crossing, because the crosser can't fly straight anyway.
A flyer's first clean crosswise crossing earns applause from the whole flying hall, at any age, and grown-ups pretend it means nothing to them.
Adults who drop something still say 'anti' under their breath, exactly as they did at four. It's the one childish habit nobody gets teased for.
Because a whisper carries in heliox, private things are written on scraps of paper and passed under the table, and reading one aloud is about the worst manners there are.
Every block keeps one felt-hung room for quarrels, since a raised voice in a bare arcade rings for three corridors.
Lullabies are sung through a fold of felt held to the mouth. It takes the brightness off a heliox voice, and makes every parent sound like an old recording.
Players carry their 1.2-metre flutes upright through crowded arcades, and people step aside for them as they would for a ladder.
A visiting choir's first act in any hall is to sing one long note and listen, because every room rings at its own pitch in heliox, and you sing to the room.
On their tenth birthday children are played one recording from the old air. They laugh at the voices spoken through a blanket until someone tells them what was being said.
The first thing a host does is hand a guest something warm to hold, because the helium will have drawn the heat out of their hands on the way over.
Bad news is told in the baths, where everyone is warm and nobody can storm off without dripping.
Laundry goes on at one in the morning, when kWh are cheapest, and a household that runs its machines at lamp-noon gets talked about.
The twenty minutes by the light panel before school are when most families have their only quiet talk of the day, so worlds stay off at the panel.
Keel night crews eat breakfast at two in the morning in the Quayside cafes, and day people who stay up to join them are treated as tourists.
Every block keeps a pot on the 65 °C loop that never comes off. Anyone may take a ladle, so long as they put something back.
Someone starting a new job puts a jar of black garlic on the loop that day. It takes five weeks, and by then they know whether to open it with friends or alone.
When someone is upset, a friend sets a vat-egg custard on the hot tap and sits with them until it's done. That takes about an hour, which is the point.
Amazake brewed overnight on the warm loop is the morning-after drink, and handing someone a cup tells them you noticed.
Hall servers carry full trays antispinward round the room and bring the empties back spinward, which they claim saves them about an egg's weight a trip.
Where high decks are allotted by age, 'gone up' means retired, and the move is made in a single day with the whole corridor carrying.
In crowded drums the baths never close, and the four-in-the-morning bath, when one shift meets the next, is where the block's news changes hands.
Whichever side loses the vote over a block's atrium light gets to choose the lamps' colour for the year. Colour costs nothing, and losers should have something.
Nobody claps a painted dawn until the far bank is fully lit. Clapping early marks you as a visitor, and the painter will mention it.
It's bad manners to ask whose dawn it is until it's over, because the painter is usually standing next to you.
A painted dawn is played once and never again, so people who missed a great one ask people who saw it, and the telling improves every year.
At a painted dusk the audience keeps its hand lamps dark until the painter's last colour has gone, then switches them on all at once.
Apprentice lamp-painters are given the first ten minutes of the dawn, when nobody important is watching. The old painters always are.
The herb shelf's lamp is the last light switched off in a flat being left, and the first switched on in the new one, before the bags are down.
The last person out of a hall at night leaves one hand lamp on low by the door, for whoever comes up from the Keel shift.
The lake belongs to the elders until the sunline is a quarter up, and young swimmers wait on the steps pretending to stretch.
Couples who want to be alone climb the end-wall terraces, where the light is thinnest, and find that everyone else had the same idea.
A Hollow hour is given folded inside a card with a sprig of something green, and the card is kept long after the hour is spent.
When someone is ill at home, friends turn their own lamps down for an hour a day and send the kWh over, so the sickroom can be bright.
It's rude to remark on how bright someone's flat is. It's like asking what they're paid.
On a child's birthday the household lamps go whatever colour the child likes. It costs nothing, and it's always the first thing they ask for.
Whoever has the brightest room on a corridor hosts the sewing evening, and brings out the good chairs, which are also the oldest.
Reading lamps are kept a warm amber in the lamp-night. Anyone reading by white light is assumed to be studying for something.
Children pollinate the blossom on the block's fruit trees with soft brushes, and each child's brush hangs in the school with their name on it long after they've left.
'Look past the line' is the first thing every child is taught in the Hollow: the far bank, never the sunline.
The children who help wrap a block's pear trees in their chilled tents are the only ones allowed to unwrap them, six weeks later.
Where beds are shared in shifts, whoever gets up leaves the lamp at the colour the next sleeper likes.
On the day the terrace rents come back to everyone, strangers thank each other for the dawns.
A painted dawn is applauded by raising slates, which makes no sound and somehow says more.
In the dim woods a hand lamp goes on only to read a slate, and is cupped in the other hand while you read.
Children choose the adult who'll take them to the Window years in advance, and are allowed to change their mind exactly once.
In the twenty minutes of red light before the shutter opens, the adult tells the child one true thing they have never told anyone, and the child keeps it.
Nobody comes back from the Window able to say what it was like, so schools ask the children to draw it, and the drawings stay up until the next class goes.
A back-crew hand's patch, with its band of tiny stitched stars, is given away to a child on the way home from their Window, and never sold.
Back crews are served first at any table they sit at, because they're the only ones who see what all the metal fell out of.
After the Window a child's cuffs are re-dyed bruise, the brown-violet of the River's dust, and other children know without asking.
Back crews bet on how long a raft's edge will take to cover a chosen star, and the pot goes to the crew's Knotnight table.
When an apple is cut crosswise, the youngest at the table counts the points of the star aloud, and everyone acts surprised that it's five again.
People point aft, toward the back end wall, when they talk about the stars, since that's where the Windows are. Visitors think they're pointing at a wall.
A drum without a Window of its own books its eight-year-olds into a neighbour's, and the neighbour's guide always asks them first what they expect to see.
On the way home from the Window the child asks what the adult saw at eight, and the adult says 'the same', which is true: the River has hardly moved in a lifetime.
Most children choose one of their aunts to take them to the Window, and their parents say they don't mind.
Everyone in a glide car lifts their feet at the catch. It does nothing, and everyone does it.
When the cradle lets go, the whole car says the name of the drum ahead, so it knows they're coming.
From a glide car's windows you can watch the drum you've left grow small, and the custom is to say goodbye to it out loud, once.
On every glide, children count the rings of quay lights, and the number is never the same twice.
Elders too old for the catch send something from their herb shelf in their place, and it's given their seat at the table.
Elders who do glide hold the hand of whoever is next to them at the catch, stranger or not, and nobody minds.
A child's first glide is to the nearest neighbour and straight back, and the ring counter at the far end gives first-gliders a second rice ball.
A wanderer's card is read aloud at their table on the day it lands, light delay and all.
A guest who stays leaves a spoon of their own starter, registered at the Gate, and takes a spoon of the house's.
Guests bring herbs from their own shelf, cut that morning. Never gin: it's too cheap to say anything.
Wanderers leave a herb cutting in the guest flat when they go, which is why Margin flats have the strangest shelves on the row.
People thank the Gate crew on the way in, because a phage stopped at the Gate is a famine that didn't happen.
When a family starter dies, the strain library grows it back from its file within a week, and the household sits with the old crock for an evening anyway.
Visitors are asked at every ring counter whose broth is better, theirs or ours, and the only polite answer is 'yours, today'.
Two people arguing about broth must each glide to the other's ring counter before the argument is allowed to go on.
On the slow line the oldest rider in a car is called aunt, whatever their sex, and is asked to settle arguments, mostly about broth.
Weightless riders never set a bulb of soup down, since there is no down. They hand it on, and a bulb drifting loose is everyone's job and nobody's fault.
When two households swap drums, each leaves its herb shelf planted for the other, so the first meal in a new home is seasoned by strangers.
Anyone who goes express is expected to come back with a story worth five days of wallet, and the table decides whether it was.
Slow-line riders keep the clock of the last drum they slept in, so in a long car three people can disagree about whether it's breakfast.
The last cup of the night at a ring counter is the strongest, having sat on the loop all day, and it's saved for whoever comes in on the last glide.
The release is marked in silence: everyone in the car writes the next drum's name on a slate and holds it up to the drum they're leaving.
Wanderers like to stand by the Ledger as they come through the ring and watch the night's guest count go up by one.
The year's best kite is hung over a station ring platform, so every arrival walks in under it.
On the way to school, children read the Count aloud the way other children read shop signs.
Ring counters keep a chalk board of bets on the date of par, and the winner buys broth for the whole platform, which is free anyway.
People touch the Count board on the way past whenever it ticks down past a round number, the way others touch a lucky step.
The oldest at the table lifts their lid first, and nobody else lifts theirs until they hear it.
Lids are lifted toward yourself, so the steam goes into your own face and not your neighbour's.
A lid put back on a half-eaten plate means 'I'm coming back', and clearing it is a small crime.
A child who forgets their lid is said to be feeding the room, since the room gets the heat.
The cook lifts the first lid at the head of the table, and the sound of four hundred lids follows it down the room.
An apple is never eaten by one person. It's cut crosswise, the star is shown, and it's shared by at least two.
Whoever cuts the apple takes the smaller half, so apples are cut very carefully.
'Have some Nine' is said to anyone who looks peaky, and sliding the pot across the table means the conversation is over.
The Nine goes round the table antispinward, 'so it's lighter for the next person', which is true by about a hair.
Cooks add the Nine at the table, never in the pot ('don't brown your lysine'), and a cook who forgets eats the bitter batch.
On a blight anniversary the halls cook the blight menu again, and the young complain that it's better than the usual.
People date their lives by blight vintages: married in the crackling year, moved up in the starch-cheese year.
Before a new larder is made, the old one is eaten at a larder supper, and whoever finds the oldest jar names next year's preserve.
At a birthday dinner the person whose day it is serves the salad, because serving the dearest dish is the honour.
Salad is always cut at the table, in front of everyone, so nobody need wonder about portions.
A tomato is cut into as many slices as there are people, however thin that makes them.
Pastry is never brought as a gift. It's what everyone eats every day, and turning up with it says you forgot.
A host who sees a guest pour a fifth gin brings out a bowl of jook without a word, and the guest eats it without a word.
A first flat's herb shelf is planted from cuttings brought by everyone who helped with the move, so no two shelves start alike.
The heel of every loaf goes to whoever is leaving soonest, for the road.
Diners stand when the cook comes out of the kitchen, because they've been eating someone's hours.
Nothing is left in a bowl at the Mill table. The food was free, so leaving it says you only came for the company.
A cultivated steak is carved by whoever is newest at the table, so they learn early how thin it can go.
The first slice off a household loaf goes to whoever fed the starter that week.
At the Mill table people write 'pass the Nine' on their slates instead of asking, and the slate travels with the pot.
On weekdays nobody eats with their own household: you sit where the table puts you, which is how half the marriages start.
A new cook's first service is eaten in silence until the last lid is down, and then the whole room bangs the table.
A new broth is tried on the block every {weekday}, and the vote is counted in second cups.
Every cup in the hall is someone's practice piece, and guests are expected to guess the year it was made.
An apprentice's first lid that fits properly is set on the hall's stockpot, and stays there until a better one comes along.
Where the Mill Hall runs four sittings, you give up your seat the moment your lid is down.
Crowded corridors keep one shared herb shelf by the lift, and the rule is cut a sprig, water the pot.
Guests on guest-right are served first at the long table and lift their lids last.
Where Hollow hours go at auction, a bought hour is given with its price torn off the card, and everyone guesses it anyway.
Every owner of a coat adds one mend in their own colour of thread, so an old coat reads like a family tree, down to the crooked orange patch nobody will own up to.
A mend is shown, never hidden: gold thread on a torn cuff, a bright patch on a knee. Hiding one is thought faintly dishonest, like pretending a coat is new.
Each time a growing seam is let out, the date is inked inside the hem, so trousers handed down three times carry a small ladder of birthdays.
A remade sofa keeps one square of its old cover sewn inside the new one, where only the next remaker will find it. Remakers say they have found them four deep.
At a wedding, whoever remade the couple's sofa stands up and says what the frame has been. "A bed, a bench, a bed again" is the kind of history that gets a cheer.
The oldest chair in the room goes to the guest. It is an honour, because the oldest chair is usually the best one, and a small test, because it is also the one most often re-glued.
Heirlooms get names once they pass a hundred years, usually after whoever first sat on them, cut with them or broke them, which is how a bread knife comes to be called Old Petra.
Before anything goes back to the Yards to be remade, someone in the household says goodbye to it out loud. Children find this very funny until it is their cot.
Once a year each block judges its larders, and the judging is fierce: points for the age of the cheese and the depth of the miso, quiet sympathy for anyone whose rusks have gone soft.
Anything taken from the larder before Knotnight must be put back within the week, in front of a witness, or it doesn't count. Small children make keen witnesses and poor keepers of secrets.
Nobody lives in a new flat until its herb shelf is planted, so couples carry a pot of basil over the threshold before the furniture, even if it means a night on the floor.
When someone dies, their herb shelf stays lit for a week before anyone takes a cutting. Then the block comes for sprigs, and the shelf goes on growing in forty kitchens.
Herb lines are traced like families. Asking whose basil this is counts as polite conversation, and a line from a famous cook's shelf gets mentioned at every meal it touches.
The herb shelf is the last lamp anyone turns off in a hard month, so a dark shelf means real trouble. Neighbours who notice one bring soup, and stay to eat it so it doesn't look like charity.
Cuttings travel wrapped in a damp cloth in a breast pocket, which is why so many old jackets have one pocket faintly green inside.
Second-hand stalls price a thing by its story as well as its weight. A coat with three named owners fetches more than one with none, though it keeps you exactly as warm.
A child's first mend is made on their own sleeve, badly, and nobody is allowed to fix it. Adults still point theirs out at parties, the way other people show off old scars.
On {weekday} nights the block mends together: everyone brings what's torn to the hall, the good menders sit at the end of the table, and the young are handed the socks.
Offcuts are never thrown away. They go into the block's rag chest, and the usual gift for a first flat is a quilt from it, with a square from every household on the landing.
Remade things keep the old one's name if they do the same job, so plenty of families eat at a grandmother's table that has been three different tables.
Borrowing a tool comes with a small repair: a borrowed knife goes back honed, and a borrowed coat comes home with a button sewn on tighter than it left.
New things are admired by weight, never by price. "Three hundred grams of new" is how you praise a lining, and everyone does the sum in their head.
Children get a larder shelf of their own at about six and must keep it stocked from their own pocket. Most stock it with sugar glass and guard it fiercely.
The first plant on a new herb shelf is chosen by the oldest person at the flat-warming, and elders nearly always choose chives or mint, which nobody has ever managed to kill.
Clothes are re-dyed for big days rather than replaced. The block's dye vat runs all week before a festival, and you can tell who left it late by their purple hands.
Household account books are kept on paper and handed down, and grandchildren reading them find that a sofa cost exactly what a sofa costs now.

Children are often named for the dead whose shares they carry, and a note goes to the dead person's family on the date each year. Some families have swapped notes for so long that nobody remembers who wrote first.
At a naming the dead's family brings a gift, usually a remade heirloom, and both names are read out together: the baby's, and the person whose share the baby carries.
Both families come down to the station ring to read a new pair of names on the Ledger together, and the dead's grandchildren usually bring the baby's first herb pot.

A child who carries a stranger's share is sometimes given the stranger's trade as a middle name, so the drum has its Tomas Gatekeepers and Runa Bakers. Most drop it at twelve and take it back at forty.
At a funeral each mourner brings a sprig from their own shelf, and the sprigs go into one broth that everybody drinks at the end. People say it tastes of the whole block.
Close family go dark for three days after a death, black threads on their left wrists, and the block takes turns sitting by their door to explain to callers.
The last pot from a dead person's herb shelf is kept alive for whoever carries their share, and handed over at the naming with the soil still damp.
Someone with no children who names a young couple as heir says so in public, at the block court. The couple cook the giver dinner every week after that, and it is the best-fed old age in the drum.
Where a birth right can be given but not sold, the child grows up calling the giver second mother or second father, and keeps them the best seat at every birthday.
Where birth rights can be sold, the seller is thanked by name at the naming, and the child sends them a card every birthday. More than a few of these turn into friendships.
The fitting at fourteen comes with a family dinner, and the custom is to cook the child's favourite and say nothing about why. Everyone knows; the dumplings are the point.
The first time part of a child's dividend goes into their own name, they buy one thing with it in front of the family. It is almost always food, and usually for someone else.
At eighteen, with the whole dividend in their own name, young people buy one hour of someone else's time, a haircut, a lesson or a cooked meal, and must say at dinner whether it was worth it.
Funerals end with the share being read back to the drum: the deck, the years, the work, and the name of whoever held it before.
Some families mark the anniversary of the stranger whose share their child carries by cooking the stranger's favourite dish, then send the stranger's family a picture of the plate.
A baby's first taste at the naming is a dab of the Nine on a fingertip, so the first thing the drum ever says to a new person is "have some Nine".
At a naming the child's table stands up one at a time, parents last, and each aunt promises one particular thing: to teach knots, to explain the Glide, to be the one who isn't shocked.
When an elder moves up to the high decks, the block walks them to the cab and calls it going up. The elder is expected to grumble about the move and secretly time the new walk to the Hollow.
Elders who die with Hollow hours unspent leave them by name, and the heirs are expected to use them in one go, on the dead's favourite bench.
New babies are announced with a sweet in every bowl at the Mill Hall's breakfast, and people go round asking whose until someone admits it.

A family in mourning is given a morning in the Hollow, whatever the rota or the auction says, to walk once round the floor without talking. At half a g the nine and a half kilometres take about two hours, which is the point.
Nobody says that someone died. They say she went back to the drum, which is gentle, and also exactly true.
Couples who draw a licence in the lottery tell their parents first and everyone else much later, since half the people they know drew nothing.
Under a birth stop, cots go from flat to flat round the block, remade when they need it, with every baby's name stitched into the lining. Some carry a dozen names from four decks.
For a month after a death the cooked hall lays the dead's place at the long table, lid on. At the end of the meal the youngest at the table eats what's under the lid, and it counts as an honour.
Notes to the dead's family are handwritten on paper because they are meant to be kept, and families keep them in the larder with the other things that must last through a Dark.
Someone always plays the dead person's least favourite song at the funeral, badly, so that everybody laughs once.
Newborns are carried up to the Hollow floor once in their first month, so their first half-g is in someone's arms. Grandparents on the high decks insist on it, and swear the baby noticed.
When a flat passes to a grandchild, the grandchild sleeps one night in the grandparent's bed before anything in it is moved.
A Margin flat lent to a young couple comes with a full larder from the block. The couple's first job is to plant the herb shelf, and their second is to complain about the last couple's.
The family's oldest object is put into the baby's hands for a moment at the naming, so the newest person in the household has held the oldest thing in it.
When a household's third child arrives, the landing cooks for it one evening each for a month, since everyone knows exactly how small the flat just got.
On Booking Day everyone guesses the year's beam before it is read. It is nearly always flat, so the prize goes to whoever said "flat" with the straightest face.
The Booking Day question is argued at every table for a month, and the rule is that you must make the other side's case once, out loud, before you may vote against it.
The Booking Day feast is paid for with the Quiet's savings, so dinner is the day of talking turned into steak, salad and half an apple. Elders point this out every year.
At breakfast on Booking Day each household reads its meter aloud: what it drew last year and what it means to do with the next. Teenagers find this unbearable, and do it themselves at forty.
Children born on Booking Day are called harvest babies and are expected to make a speech at the feast once they can talk. Some are still making it at ninety.
The first glass at the Booking Day feast is raised toward the front end wall, because that is where the power comes in.

On the Quiet the halls are full by lamp-dawn and nobody brings anything to read. The rule is to talk to someone you have never spoken to, which in a block of three thousand is still possible at eighty.
Old arguments are settled on the Quiet, out loud, with the table listening. Anything settled then stays settled, and raising it again costs the raiser a round of tea.
The Quiet is when the young tell the old about the worlds they live in and the old tell the young about the Eleven Days, and both sides pretend it is the first time they've heard it.
The Quiet ends at midnight, when everyone's worlds come back on at once, and the custom is to send your first message to someone you talked to that day.
Each block flies the Long Flight together behind its oldest flier, hand lamps all one colour, so from the end walls you can pick out your own block in the river of lights.
People who don't fly the Long Flight sit on the elders' terraces with gin and judge the fliers. A wobbly crosswise turn gets a groan you can hear from the axis.
A first-timer on the Long Flight carries a hand lamp borrowed from someone who flew their own first Flight with it, and hands it back at lamp-dawn.
The Long Flight ends at lamp-dawn on the end-wall terraces, where whoever stayed up longest gets the first cup of coffee and the right to complain about it.
On Knotnight the lamps go down to a glow and the block makes the year's larder together, as if a long dark were coming. None has come in a hundred million years, and the miso is still made properly.
Knotnight's meal is whatever is fresh and won't keep: the salad, the soft cheese, the last tomatoes. In the layer era's long dark there was nothing fresh for weeks, so nothing fresh is saved.
With the lamps down on Knotnight, children hear the ring-era stories about habitats that went dark for forty days at a time, and may stay up until the last crock is sealed.
Each Knotnight crock is sealed with the date and the names of everyone who stirred it, and opened the next Knotnight to be judged. The names on a bad crock are read out too.
Every household gives one jar from its new Knotnight larder to a household that isn't family, so every larder in the block holds something of someone else's.
At Homecoming the block meets its wanderers at Station Ring {ring} with hand lamps, the table at the front, and a wanderer's first meal home is whatever they complained most about missing.
Wanderers coming home are asked one question on the platform: which broth was best. Anyone who names their own drum's is lying, and is cheered for it.
Homecoming wanderers bring back a spoon of starter, a recipe and a song, and teach the song at the first hall dinner. Some halls end the year with forty new songs and one good one.
During a Passing every hall cooks one recipe that came in from the other raft that week, and eats it without complaint, whatever it turns out to be.
When the other raft's answer to a song begins, about half an hour after the song went out, everyone stands. People have stood through some very long answers.
Children born during a Passing get a second name from a list the other raft sends, and the other raft does the same, so somewhere out there a child is named after one of this raft's soups.
On the last night of a Passing the choirs send one more song, knowing its answer will come long after everyone has gone home. Whoever has the late shift at the hall listens for it.
Founding day is kept by switching the lamps off at the rim and back on one deck at a time, rising toward the Hollow, while families wait on their landings for their own deck's turn.
Mending Day forbids buying anything new, and the halls fill with sewing machines and lathes. Everyone brings one broken thing; the best menders bring three, to show off.
On swap day each block lays out what it no longer needs along its arcade, and anyone may take whatever they can carry up three decks by the stairs, which keeps the sofas where they are.
Children are weighed twice on Weighing Day, at the rim and on the Hollow floor, and told they lost half of themselves on the way up. A few cry; most ask to go again.
On the anniversary of the Eleven Days the lamps go out for an hour, as they did then, and everyone old enough to remember is asked to say one thing about it. The list gets shorter every year.
Row Day remembers the row's drums being founded together: the ring counters swap broths with the next drum along, and everyone drinks a neighbour's and finds fault with it.
The first apple off the drum's oldest tree each year goes to whichever block drew it in the lottery, and is cut crosswise at its hall so the star can go down the table hand to hand.
Each of a child's aunts takes one evening a week, so a child with a busy table may eat in five kitchens and be told off in five different styles.
Aunts are aunts whatever their sex, and every adult knows the particular voice a child uses to say "Aunt {name}" when it wants something.
Eating alone in a cooked hall is allowed, and so unusual that the cook comes out to sit with you, which is exactly why nobody does it.
In a cooked hall you take the next free seat, not your choice of one, so half the friendships in the drum began with someone asking for the Nine.
Complaints about noise at the block court must be made in a whisper. In heliox a whisper carries across the atrium anyway, and it keeps tempers down.
At the block court anyone who has spoken twice must wait until three others have spoken once. The timekeeper is usually a twelve-year-old, who enjoys it enormously.
Anyone drawn for the assembly by lot is handed a list of complaints by their block court to take along, then a second, much shorter list of the ones that matter.
Whoever is drawn for the assembly gets a cake from their block on the day, and a year of being asked what is really going on.
Going dark is announced by tying on the black thread at breakfast, in front of the household, so nobody can say they weren't told.
Friends of someone who has gone dark leave a paper notebook by their door, and the dark one reads it all at once when the thread comes off, like a long letter from the whole block.
The black thread means don't message me. It doesn't mean don't knock, and people who go dark get more visitors in a week than most get in a month.
Long letters are read once. When one lands from another raft, the family reads it aloud at the table together, then puts it away and never opens it again.
Some long letters from the far side of the Shade are addressed simply to whoever is eating in a certain hall, years after they were written, and the hall reads them aloud over the night stew.
A long letter is written over many evenings and never corrected once the last line is down, because a correction is a lie about how you felt that night.
Wedding guests give Hollow hours rather than things, and compare minutes out loud all evening while the couple pretend not to keep count.
The wedding apple is cut crosswise by the oldest guest, who holds up the star and says where they first saw a real one: a Window, a back-crew shift, or never.
Gifts are reckoned in kWh, and the polite thing is to guess a present's cost too low. Guessing right is rude, and guessing high is an accusation.
Wanderers send a card home from every row, and the table pins them up in order with the light delay written on each, so the kitchen wall becomes a map of how far away the child got.
Cards home are answered the day they arrive, one line only, so a wanderer collects a trail of one-liners across the raft: the basil is fine; your aunt misses you; the basil is not fine.
Gifted Hollow hours are spent with the giver the first time, which is why people give them to the people they want to see.
When someone moves into a block, each household gives them an hour of something: a haircut, a lesson, a cooked meal. A newcomer can live very well for a month on hours.
Gossip lives in the baths, by long agreement. What's said in the steam stays there, mostly, and what doesn't is blamed on the steam.
Big favours are repaid in time, never kWh: an evening's cooking, a mended coat, a morning holding a ladder. Paying kays for a favour is the polite way to end a friendship.
Nobody asks a childless adult when they're having children. They ask what they're making, teaching or cooking, and settle in for a long answer.
People write on their slates and hand them across instead of speaking, so an argument is two people writing faster and faster until one of them laughs.
A silent hour follows the evening meal, when even the halls only clatter. Once a year the children may break it, and they spend the whole hour shouting.
A retiring woodwarden walks her successor past every tree she kept, without a word, and at the end hands over her slate with one tree's name on it: the one to watch.
A child's first slate comes at five, and the first word written on it is chosen by their table. It is never hello.
Every cook has a song, and the hall sings it when that cook's dish comes out. Dead cooks still get theirs whenever somebody makes their recipe.
Every long table keeps one seat for whoever wanders in, and a stranger who takes it owes the table one story before pudding.
Most households spend a little of the returned rents on a seat at a painted dusk, so the money goes round once and comes back as a show.
The drum votes for its best dawn of the year by raising hand lamps on the terraces, and the painter counts them from the lawn below and always loses count.
When a dawn is a famous one, people dye something the colour of its best minute and wear it for a week, so the arcades turn rose all at once.
An apprentice's first finished piece is given to the first stranger who admires it. Apprentices learn quickly which corridors the visitors use.
Pieces carry their maker's mark and year, and every later mend gets its mender's mark beside it, so an old chair can carry a dozen signatures down one back leg.
Buyers who glide in are expected to watch an hour of the making first, so they know what they are paying for. The makers also like an audience.
There is no Margin here and no fuss about it. The Booking Day toast is "par, and a good year", said in the tone of an old joke.
Families eat in sittings at a shared table, and the last sitting washes up for everyone. Everybody wants the early sitting and nobody admits it.
Each landing shares one long herb shelf with a tag on every pot. A leaf may be taken without asking; a whole sprig of basil is a matter for the landing.
Shared beds are made up with the next sleeper's own sheet, folded at the foot by the last, which is the politest thing two strangers can do for each other.
In the bunk rooms children sleep stacked by age, except on birthdays, when the birthday child gets the top bunk and the whole room's attention.
On licence lottery day the halls serve the same dish to everyone, so no table can tell from the food who drew a licence and who didn't.
A new baby is carried round the whole block in its first week, so that everyone gets to see one.
