goods.t: Allots its high decks and Hollow hours by age, so the old have the lake every lamp-dawn.
Auctions its high decks and Hollow hours and spends the rents on a longer noon.
Gives its Hollow hours by lottery and in festivals, and lends its high-deck flats by need.
Allots its high decks by years of service: Gate staff, back crews and teachers go up first.
Rotates every deck through the Hollow in turn, six hours every eight weeks, and nobody may sell a turn.
Auctions half its Hollow hours and draws the other half by lottery, so money buys only half the lake.
Lets each block vote on how to share its Hollow hours, so no two blocks do it the same way.
Auctions its high decks and pays the rents back to everyone as an extra dividend on Booking Day.
Gives the high decks to elders and the Hollow's bright half to families with children under eight.
Allots by need: the ill, the very old and new parents first, then a lottery for everyone else.
Pays for Hollow hours in work: one hour of light for every four given to the halls, the nurseries or the old.
Lets high-deck flats pass down with a family's places, so some families have looked onto the Hollow for twenty generations.
Lets its high-deck flats at a fixed rent set every Booking Day, with a waiting list instead of an auction.
Trades Hollow hours on an open exchange, but caps any household at three hours a week.
Gives every resident an equal ration of Hollow tokens, which can be swapped or given but never sold.
Gives every resident an equal ration of Hollow tokens that can be sold, so the young sell theirs and buy express legs.
Allots by age, but every child gets a free Hollow day on their birthday.
Counts years lived in the drum, not years of age, so a newcomer of sixty starts at the bottom.
Draws its high-deck flats by lottery every ten years, and everyone moves when the draw comes in.
Auctions the Hollow's hours of full sun and gives the dawn and dusk hours free to anyone who turns up.
Auctions the bright hours and lets the lamp-night go by queue, first come, first in.
goods.short: sold by day, queued by night

goods.t: Allots by honours: a decade on the back crews, a childless calling or a share given away earns a high-deck flat.
Gives its high decks to the childless and its Hollow hours to children, and calls that fair both ways.
Moves whole blocks up in turn by lottery, so a neighbourhood climbs to the high decks together for twenty years.
Auctions its high decks, but only among people over sixty, so money and age both have to agree.
Leaves the Hollow open to anyone at any hour; whoever is there is there, and the crowd is half the point.
Prices Hollow hours by brightness: lamp-noon costs most, the last hour of dusk almost nothing.
Allots by deck, a turn every eight weeks, and lets elders join any turn they like.
Changes its rule by referendum every twenty years; this generation is trying half auction, half age.
Gives high-deck flats to whoever has spent the most hours caring for others, counted on the drum's books.
Auctions its Hollow hours and spends the rents on the halls, so whoever buys noon pays for everyone's dinner.
goods.short: at auction, rents to the halls

goods.t: Allots high decks by age and Hollow hours by work: the Keel crews, who spend their shifts under plain lamps, get the most.
goods.short: decks by age, hours by work

births.t: Places and shares pass in the family, and a child born ahead of a death waits for a share.
Pools every share at death and gives each share one birth right, which can be given away but never sold.
Pools its places and lets birth rights be sold, so a third child is something a family saves for.
Holdings, warmly run: young couples marry into lent Margin flats and wait for a share to free with a home already made.
Holdings with a share-gift custom: the childless adopt a young couple from outside their family as heirs, and say so in public.
Licenses births by lottery during a stop; couples who both hold places enter, first children first.
Fits a reversible implant at fourteen during the stop, removed at the clinic when a licence comes.
Pools its places and sends every unused birth right to a yearly lottery, so a third child is luck.
Holdings, and a third child on thin shares is nobody's business but the household's.
Holdings, where three children came back into fashion and the households have got thinner for it.
Holdings, with adult heirs adopted freely, so a childless household can keep its places by choosing a friend.
Prices births rather than forbidding them: proofreading is free for licensed births and charged for the rest.
Holds births to deaths by custom alone: two each, and a third only with a death in the household and the family's blessing.
Pools its places and gives each spare place to the longest-waiting couple on a public list.
Licenses births by lottery but posts an end date for the stop, {n} years off, and means to keep it.
Pools its places; a childless resident's unused right is theirs to give, and giving one is the grandest gift in the drum.
births.short: pool, rights given by the childless

births.t: Lets a couple who win a licence give it to another couple, but never sell it.
Holdings, and the register tells each family whose share the new child carries, so the child can take their name.
Counts since a blight hit its overspent households; licences go to couples who both hold places, and the young bet on the date of par.
Holdings again since a stop that ended {ago} years ago; the old Count board hangs in a museum as a warning to itself.
Holdings with a Margin that a supermajority may spend on births once after a disaster, and then rebuild over a generation.
Pools its places, and each child's birth right is held in trust until they turn twenty, then theirs to use or give.

gin.t: Sells gin near cost with thiamine in it, as in the salt.
Taxes spirits hard and posts the methanol warnings on every platform of the Quaysides.
Taxes gin lightly and sells it only in the halls after six, where someone is always cooking.
Rations spirits by card, a bottle a week each, and the card can't be lent.
Pours gin free at funerals and namings and sells it at cost the rest of the year.
Sells gin at cost by the glass but never by the bottle, so nobody drinks alone by accident.
Taxes spirits and spends the duty on the clinics; its methanol deaths rose for it, and it argues about that every Booking Day.
Lets each visitor bring two bottles duty-free, so its neighbours never arrive with fewer than two.
Sells beer and wine freely but no spirits, and its Gate tests every bottle that comes in for methanol.
Taxes drink by strength, so the drum drinks long and weak: lager, sours, gin at half the usual proof.
Sells gin at cost from the Mill Halls and nowhere else, so all drinking is done in company.
Taxes gin a little and hands out free methanol test strips with every bottle.
Sells gin at cost to anyone over twenty and not at all to anyone younger.
Gives everyone a small free ration on Booking Day and sells the rest at cost.
Lets each block set its own gin price, and everybody knows which atrium is cheapest.
Taxes gin hard but sells Mill lager at cost, which has made it a beer drum.
Sells gin near cost with thiamine, and a clinic nurse calls round on anyone buying a bottle a day.
Tried a gin tax for ten years, counted its methanol deaths, and went back to selling near cost with thiamine.
Allows spirits only in the high-deck bars, where a fall carries half the energy it would at the rim.
Taxes the bottle but not the glass, so gin is cheap in company and dear alone.
Keeps gin at cost but closes every bar at midnight and serves jook to whoever is left.

guests.t: Guests get one hour on the floor a day, bright half or dim, their choice.
Guests may buy Hollow hours at the residents' auction price, which runs about 3 kWh at lamp-noon.
Guests go into the daily lottery with everyone else, one ticket each.
The Hollow opens to guests only in the lamp-night, when the Spindle opens and the floor is quiet.
The end-wall terraces are open to guests at any hour; the floor is for residents.
A guest's first hour is free; after that it's 2 kWh an hour, paid to the deck whose turn it is.
Guests join whichever deck has its turn that day, as if they lived there.
The first hour of the dawn ramp is kept for guests, who are thought to appreciate it most.
Guests may use the end-wall terraces and the flying halls above them, but the floor is booked.
An hour at lamp-noon costs a guest 5 kWh, and the rent goes to the halls.
Guests draw a lottery ticket on each night of their stay; about one in three wins an afternoon.
Once the dusk ramp ends, guests may walk the floor and picnic by hand lamp until midnight.
Elders give their spare Hollow hours to guests at the ring counter; ask, and someone usually has one.
Hollow hours are sold to anyone by the half-hour, and guests pay what residents pay, about 4 kWh an hour at noon.
The top terraces, where a child can jump the height of a house, are kept for guests; the floor is booked months ahead.
Guests get one free hour on their third night, which the drum calls the leaving hour.
Guests may fly the Spindle and walk the floor on any lamp-night, but never by day.
The Hollow is auctioned and guests bid like anyone else; an hour at dusk goes for about a kWh.
Guests are drawn by lottery for the bright half, and those who lose get the lamp-night instead.
Guests may use the end-wall terraces and the kite slopes, which the drum keeps open to everyone.
Any hall's Hollow picnic will make room for a guest, and the halls always ask.
An hour on the floor costs a guest 6 kWh, the price of a cook's hour, and the drum doesn't apologise.
Guests may walk the floor only after the sunline is out, and a warden with a hand lamp shows them round.
Guests enter a weekly draw for a full bright-half turn, read out at the ring counter on {weekday}s.
Guests get the back end wall's terraces, where the light is gentler and the whole floor is in view.
Residents may sign one guest per household into their own turn, and most do.
A guest hour costs 2 kWh, and half of it goes back to whoever gave up the slot.
Guests may use the Hollow in the last hour of dusk and through the lamp-night, when it costs nothing to light.
Guests are entered in the evening draw at their inn, and the innkeeper reads out the winners at breakfast.
Guests may use the terrace gardens near the axis, which residents rarely book because the light up there is thin.

day.t: Lamps up at 06:30, like most drums, warm to white over twenty minutes.
Lamps up at 05:30, an hour ahead of the row, so its bread is through the Quaysides before anyone else's.
Lamps up at 07:30; the drum keeps late hours so its evenings overlap its neighbours' lamp-nights, and their night owls glide in.
Lamps up at 06:00, rung in by a bell in the Keel that sounds in every lift lobby.
Lamps up at 05:00 because the Keel shifts start at six, and the drum decided long ago to keep their hours.
Lamps up at 08:00; the drum runs its machines hard before dawn, sleeps in, and is not sorry.
Lamps up at 06:30 on working days and 08:00 on rest days, so the whole drum lies in together.
Lamps up at 07:00 over forty minutes, because the drum once voted that waking should take as long as a pot of tea.
Lamps up at 06:00 in homes and an hour later in the arcades, so the streets stay quiet while people eat.
Lamps up at 05:45 on the Low decks, where the schools are, and later as you climb, until the elders' decks wake at 08:00.
Lamps up at 06:30, but the working day is four hours long and the afternoons belong to the halls.
Lamps up at 09:00; the drum keeps a late clock, and its lamp-night markets are the liveliest on the row.
Lamps up at 06:30, half an hour into the Hollow's dawn, so early risers on the terraces catch the gold before work.
Lamps up at 04:30 for half the drum and 10:30 for the other half: it runs two days in one and shares its halls and baths between them.
Lamps up at 07:15, after the night's laundry and the Yards' busy hours have wound down.
Lamps up at 06:00, and nobody starts work until their block has eaten breakfast together.
Lamps up at 05:30, on a clock set for the vat shifts four centuries ago that nobody has dared to move.
Lamps up at 06:45, with a twenty-minute dim after lunch that the drum calls the turning.
Lamps up at 07:00, timed to the first glide train of the day, which a good part of the drum rides to work next door.
Lamps up at 05:00 for the bakers and 06:30 for everyone else, and the bakers say this is the natural order.
Lamps up at 08:30; the drum works late into the evening, and its Hollow dusk is timed to supper.

history.t: lost a row of radiator panels long ago and dimmed every arcade by a third for a month to keep the heat down; a gloomy evening is still called a panel night
had a vat fire in the Keel {ago} years ago that took two dairy lines, and keeps the scorched lid of Vat Nine as a doorstop at the Gate
sprang a leak in its moat within living memory, and the crews who sealed it have a bench by the Hollow lake with their names cut into the back
lost a cryocooler bank {ago} years ago and watched the jacket gauges creep up for six days until spares came over by glide from {nb}
ate a blight menu for {n} weeks {ago} years ago, when a phage kept coming back through the cheese lines, and the dish that got everyone through, fried crackling curd, is now its festival food
had a spar fault {ago} years ago that left the Hollow dark for {n} weeks, and people born that year are still called spar-born
had a cradle jam on Station Ring {ring} for a whole booking year, and the Quaysides there became the best market in the drum while nobody could leave from them
lost a coolant pump in the back axle {ago} years ago and ate the Mill table cold for a week to keep the heat down; cold jook is still served on the date, and still disliked
owes its mycelium line to a Gate clerk called {name}, who held back a crate of {nb}'s mushrooms for a second test {ago} years ago and found the phage in it
let a phage through the Gate in a jar of pickles, once, and the Gate has asked every guest about pickles ever since
lost power to its lift cores for two days {ago} years ago, and the stair race started that week, rim to Hollow, is still run every year
flooded the Keel to the ankles when a water-works valve stuck open, and the flood mark is painted on a wall at Station Ring {ring}, very low
lost its strain library's cold room for a night {ago} years ago, and people came down from every deck with their family crocks so it could restock
drained its Hollow lake for a hull inspection {ago} years ago and found three hundred years of dropped things on the bottom, all a little antispinward of the jetty
ran every home an hour late for a month after a fault in its lamp clock, and a few blocks liked it so much they never changed back
had its Window shut for {n} years while the gallery was rebuilt, and every child who turned eight in that time was taken to {nb}'s instead
lost a whole Vat hall to a phage {ago} years ago and scrubbed it clean with volunteers, whose names are on the hall doors in their own handwriting
still counts the four marriages that came out of the evening a line deck lost power and left cabs stopped between berths
held the sunline at full through two lamp-nights when a dimmer stuck, and paid for it with a month of dim arcades that nobody minded
lost every pear in its Courts to a mould {ago} years ago and regrew them from cuttings it had once given {nb}, which {nb} sent back with a note
banned gin for a week out of nerves when a seal wept in its methanol tank farm, which everyone now agrees was the wrong way round
lost its seed store to damp {ago} years ago and rebuilt it from whatever people had growing on their herb shelves, so its coriander is still called shelf coriander
ate a month of young cheese in a week when the cold rooms in its cheese caves failed, and nobody remembers it as a disaster
put two decks' worth of people in the Hollow overnight during a scrubber fault, the only lamp-night it has ever been full
lost the colour control on its sunline for a year {ago} years ago, so every dawn came up plain white, and its lamp-painters call it the year they learned what they were for
lost its Fusarium line {ago} years ago and has eaten Neurospora steaks every anniversary since
lost its koji line {ago} years ago and rebuilt it from one family's miso crock on {street}; that family still gets the first jar of every batch
liked its yeast-blight starch custards so much that they never came off the hall menu
lost its cultured-butter line {ago} years ago and baked with Mill ghee for a month, and its elders swear the pastry was better that month
ate the Nine with everything during a three-day protein-flour blight, and still calls a short bad patch three days of Nine
keeps one vat on an old backup strain because the green-steak year, when its mycelium came out faintly green and tasted of hazelnut, beat the original
lost two vat lines in the same year {ago} years ago, and its young hall cooks still cook the double-year menu on the anniversary as a test
once lost its chocolate line for {n} weeks, which was felt more than any meat blight in its history
drank a Mill coffee so bad during a coffee blight that the blight has a name: the Brown Month
had a tomato blight {ago} years ago that made a tomato dearer than an apple for a year, and still gives a tomato to every couple who marry
renamed a square after the vat line that carried it through the blight of {ago} years ago, so people arrange to meet by Line Four
hasn't had a blight in {n} years and is quietly nervous about it
had a sourdough blight {ago} years ago and was reseeded from the genome of a starter its own wanderers had left in {far}
ate pink protein curd for a year when a backup algae line took over the flour, and curd pink is still a favourite lining colour
was fed through a long blight {ago} years ago by crates from every drum along {row}, and still sends each of them a crate of something on the date
fed {nb} through the Eleven Days, sending larder crates over by glide twice a day, and {nb} still sends a crate back every year on the date
had a choir sing on its stairs every evening of the Eleven Days, and sings the same eleven songs on the anniversary
walked its stairs for the whole of the Eleven Days, and its oldest residents can still tell you how many steps lie between their old flat and the Keel
had babies born in nearly every block during the Eleven Days, and its Dark-born, all of them seventy-four now, get the first apples on the anniversary
lost nobody in the Eleven Days and says so on a plaque at every station ring, which {nb} thinks is showing off
kept its herb shelves alive through the Eleven Days on the last of its hand lamps, and some of its basil lines still go back to those pots
sent its back crews out every day of the Eleven Days, and their names are painted in the Window gallery where the children wait in the red light
ate its larder so carefully in the Eleven Days that a third was left at the end, and gave the lot to {nb2} on the twelfth morning
is where {name} played one note on a flute at the top of every hour of the Eleven Days, on {street}, so people could tell the time; a flute still plays it there at lamp-noon
kept its halls open through the Eleven Days with nothing to cook, and people came anyway to sit at the long tables in the dark and talk
came through the Eleven Days on the thinnest shares on {row}, and its old people still keep two larders out of habit
kept its Margin through the Eleven Days without spending a share, and lent guest flats to {n} families from {nb} whose larders had run out
voted against running the cyclers fast after the Eleven Days, lost to the rest of Merrow, and still grumbles whenever anyone books an express leg
refused to tax gin when its neighbours did, {ago} years ago, and its methanol deaths have been the lowest on {row} ever since
refused to count after its blight {ago} years ago, ran thin for a generation instead, and is proud of both
refused to dim the pear Court of {block} during a radiator fault; it slowed the cabs instead, and everyone walked
refused to close its rings during a phage scare and tested every arrival at the Gate instead; that month's queue is still the longest on record
refused when {row} agreed a common lamp clock, and still keeps its own hour, which {nb} calls being late on principle
refused to let birth rights be sold when its neighbours began to, and has 'given, never sold' cut over every station ring
refused to auction its Hollow hours when it was proposed {ago} years ago, and the proposal has come back every twenty years since, like a cough
refused to close its henhouse in a lean year {ago} years ago, and the hens' great-great-granddaughters still lay on the Low decks
refused to pave its last meadow for more cab pavilions, and now has the longest walk from the cabs and the best meadow on {row}
refused to sell wedding hours in the Hollow {ago} years ago, and every wedding since has been held free on the end-wall terraces
refused to give its name back when {nb} said the founders had meant it for them, and the matter is raised, politely, at every shared festival
remembers the wedding of {name} and a back-crew hand from {nb}, {ago} years ago, where four hundred guests shared nine apples and everyone saw a star
still talks about the wedding {ago} years ago where the couple tried to meet crosswise on the Spindle, missed twice, and managed it on the third pass
named its biggest hall after {name}, a cook who fed the Quaysides for {years} years and never once took the wage
had a woodwarden called {name} who kept the same yews for {years} years and wrote one word a year on a slate; the slates hang at the edge of the wood
remembers {name}, a Gate clerk who sat with every frightened traveller for {years} years; the name is on the Ledger now, beside a baby given the same one
keeps the coat of {name}, a mender, in the museum on deck {deck}: worn by nine people and mended by all of them
has had couples leap together at weddings ever since one pair on the third-g terraces came down a hand's width spinward of the officiant and called it luck
keeps the chair of {name}, its first lamp-painter, at the foot of the back terraces, and nobody sits in it on a dawn morning
remembers a wedding during a Passing {ago} years ago, when the other raft's choir sang the vows back thirty-three minutes late, after the couple had gone to bed
had a resident called {name} who lived to {n} and spent the last ten years of it teaching children to throw anti
named a lift core after {name}, an engineer who rode every cab in it once a year for {years} years to listen to them
traded songs with a passing raft {ago} years ago and still sings one of theirs at namings, though nobody knows what the words mean
received a long letter {ago} years ago addressed to it under its founding name, which nobody had used in centuries, and read it aloud in the halls anyway
swapped two families with a passing raft {ago} years ago, its only emigrants on record, and still writes to them every Booking Day, though the letters now take weeks
taught a passing raft its broth by light, got a sour soup in return, and now serves the soup as its own
got a long letter {ago} years ago, sent {n} years before by a child on a far raft who wanted to know what a drum was like, and the whole school wrote back
saw a raft pass within half an AU {ago} years ago, the closest anyone remembers, and ran its Windows around the clock for a month
sent its lidded custard to a passing raft as a recipe and heard back, thirty-three minutes later, that they could not see what the lid was for
booked a hall for the reading of a long letter due {ago} years ago, and when the letter never came, kept the date free every year in case
wrote a long letter to a raft across the Shade {ago} years ago and expects the answer in about {n} more; the reading is already booked
remembers {painter}'s pewter dawn {ago} years ago, three hours of grey and nothing else, which half the drum walked out of and the other half still talk about
had a dusk by {painter} that ran so long through amber that lamp-night came eleven minutes late, and the clock was moved to match
still argues about the dawn {painter} painted for the first Booking Day after the Eleven Days, which came up white all at once, with no ramp at all
had its first painted dawn {ago} years ago, made by a back-crew hand who had seen the River at work and wanted everyone else to
had {painter} paint a dusk for the day its Count came down, played it once, and has never played it again
remembers the morning {painter} painted the dawn backwards, gold to violet, and the whole drum went to work feeling it was evening
voted {ago} years ago to buy a second dusk a year from {nb}'s painters, and its own have been trying to win it back since
has played the same dawn every Booking Day for {years} years, painted by someone nobody living ever met, and would not dream of changing it
has argued about the Court's light for {years} years, and the Court has won every vote, mostly because of the fig on its brightest wall
argued for a century over the colour of the sunline at full brightness, settled on a warm white by eleven votes, and still has a warm party and a cool party
spent {years} years arguing whether lids come off at the table or at the pass, and settled it by putting the lids on hinges
has argued for {years} years over whether the elders' benches belong on the front terraces or the back, and moves them every Booking Day, which pleases nobody
argued about a swell for its lake for {years} years and built half of one, which makes a single slow wave every ten minutes
has been arguing with {nb} for {n} decades over who invented the lidded rice ball, entirely in recipes
has debated for {years} years whether its lake should be warm, and keeps one end warm and the other cold in the meantime
has argued for {years} years about whether the apple at a wedding is cut by the couple or the eldest guest, and the eldest guest keeps a knife ready either way
has argued through {n} councils about whether the Nine goes in the jook or beside it, and the halls serve it both ways to keep the peace
has argued for {years} years about whether its wood should be lit at all in the lamp-night, and the woodwardens keep a dim lamp on a timer that nobody admits to setting
gave the whole Hollow to its children for one day {ago} years ago, and has done it again on the first {weekday} after Booking Day every year since
settled its gin policy by a single vote, cast by a woman who had only come in to ask about the Hollow rota
was founded with the rest of {row}, and its founding charter, kept in the Keel, is mostly about who gets the first pears
glided its whole flute section to {nb} for a concert and lost a flute in the catch; it is still on a shelf at {nb}'s platform, still in tune
voted to make its lamp-night a tenth darker and found its people slept better and argued less
had a school on deck {deck} go a whole year without a dropped cup, a record still painted on the hall wall
repainted every arcade the brown-violet of the River's edge, found it too dark to live with, and left one arcade on {street} that way
lost a spinball final to {nb} {ago} years ago on an antispinward throw that sailed over everyone, and has practised anti throws ever since
once held the Quiet for three days by mistake, when the council forgot to switch the worlds back on, and nobody complained until the third evening
planted its first birches {ago} years ago from seed grown out of a genome sent by a raft across the Shade, and still calls the wood the Letter
has kept a herb shelf in the Ledger hall for {years} years, with a cutting added at every naming
flew the Long Flight back to front one year, from the back wall toward the front, and has done it that way since because people liked flying toward the lights
once drew an assembly by lot in which two members turned out to live on the same landing, and that landing still behaves as if it runs the drum
measured its own spin one lamp-night in a school on deck {deck}, with a cup and a ruler, and the result is framed in the Keel
counted for {years} years after a vat fire, and still keeps the old Count board in the Ledger hall
came out of a birth stop {ago} years ago {n} percent under par and voted to keep the gap as its Margin, mostly on the elders' votes
spent half its Margin on births by supermajority after the Eleven Days, and finished building it back only {years} years later
took its Count down {ago} years ago and hung a Ledger in its place; the bolt holes of the old board are still in the wall, and people touch them for luck
let its last birth stop run long on purpose, by vote, to build a Margin, the first drum on {row} to do it that way
fitted its fourteen-year-olds for {years} years, and the last class to be fitted still meet every Booking Day and call themselves the Last Fourteen
keeps its old Count boards in a museum on the Quaysides, {n} of them, the oldest lettered by hand
fell one vote short of the supermajority to spend its Margin on births {ago} years ago, and both sides still claim the missing voter, who was at the baths
licensed its births by lottery for {years} years, and the lottery barrel, full of numbered balls, now draws the Hollow hours instead
took in refugees from a dark drum across the raft {ago} years ago, spent a fifth of its Margin doing it, and built it back within a generation
has held its Margin at exactly {n} percent for {ago} years, and its assembly by lot argues every year about rounding it
ended its last birth stop {ago} years ago with one naming day for every child born in the month after, and that cohort still has its own table on Booking Day
held its Count at exactly par for one day {ago} years ago before taking it down, so everyone could see it read the same number twice
claims to be the only drum on {row} that never counted, though its records go strangely thin for one decade about {ago} years ago
lent its first Margin flat to a young couple {ago} years ago, and their descendants still send the drum a pot of herbs on the date
saw {n} places given to young couples outside the givers' families on a single Booking Day {ago} years ago, when the gift swept the halls like a fashion
is {years} years into a birth stop and expects par in about {n} more; bets on the exact date are chalked on a board beside the Count
posted its first Count {years} years ago, after a long dairy blight left its thinnest households short, and the Count has fallen every year since; people check it on the way to work
started counting {years} years ago after a bad year in the vats, and hopes to hang its first Ledger before today's fourteen-year-olds turn thirty
drew its first licence lottery {years} years ago in the hall at Station Ring {ring}, and the first couple drawn still get a cheer whenever they glide home
began the fitting {years} years ago, and its first fitted class turned the day into a family dinner, which every class since has kept
is {years} years into a stop that began after a long Fusarium blight, and its Blight Kitchen has turned into the best cheap table on {row}
has been counting for {years} years, and on Booking Day it reads aloud the names of the dead whose places went unfilled that year, so nobody is forgotten before par
voted last Booking Day to end its stop early and lost by a few thousand votes, the closest it has come
had a hall cook called {name} who kept one stockpot going for {years} years, topped up and never emptied, and left it to an apprentice
lost a hall debate to {nb} on the motion that lids are a matter of upbringing, and has asked for a rematch every Booking Day since
opened its first cooked hall {ago} years ago in a freight bay on the Quaysides, and the long table there is still made from the bay's old racking
had its longest table counted at nine hundred seats, after which three halls along {row} quietly added a chair each
voted its woods silent {ago} years ago after one man's laugh carried from the front wall to the back, and he was, by all accounts, delighted
grew its yews {ago} years ago from cuttings off a single tree in {nb}, which has since died, so in a sense the whole wood is that tree
has kept a birch wood for {years} years that is wintered a strip at a time in chilled tents, so somewhere in it leaves are always falling
once went a whole year without a raised voice in its woods, and the woodwardens still argue about whether a sneeze counted
returned its terrace rents to everyone for the first time {ago} years ago, a small sum a head, and still keeps a list of what people spent it on
overspent on a light festival by a month of dim arcades, and voted to do it again
re-dyed nearly every coat in the drum the same blue for one day, and some were never changed back
ran a painted dusk every night for {years} years, one painter a night chosen by lottery, until it ran out of painters and started again
made its first famous chair {ago} years ago for a wedding in {nb}, and the chair is still there, still sat in, re-sprung {n} times
opened its craft school {ago} years ago with three benches and a lathe from a closed Keel workshop, and the lathe still turns
lost its best pattern-cutter to {far} at thirty and got her back at ninety to teach, which the school counts as a win
settled an argument about chair legs with {far} by sending a chair there by slow cycler and waiting a month for the verdict
switched from allotting its high decks by age to auctioning them {ago} years ago, and switched back {years} years later after the elders sat in the lift lobbies until it did
joined guest-right {ago} years ago after a vote that was close for a decade and then, quite suddenly, not close at all
allotted its high decks by service for {years} years, so its old back-crew hands and Gate clerks have the best views, and the habit has outlived the rule
voted against counting {ago} years ago by a wide margin and opened a swaps desk instead, which has moved a few thousand families a year ever since
has had the busiest night market on {row} for {years} years, ever since cheap lamp-night kays made it worth cooking at one in the morning
took in families from three neighbouring drums after a blight {ago} years ago and never quite thinned back out, which it takes as a compliment
has run shift-bunks in its inns since the crowding of {ago} years ago, and old bunk tickets are collected like cards
went thin in a fashion for third children {ago} years ago and has been crowded and cheerful ever since, though its Low-deck schools run two sittings

reputations.t: {nb} says {drum} would vote on the colour of the sunline if it could. It can, and does.
{drum} finds {nb} dazzling and a little vulgar, and glides over whenever it wants to be dazzled.
{nb}'s word for an over-salted stew is 'very {drum}'.
In {nb}, to 'do a {drum}' is to mend something before it has quite broken.
Ask {nb} and it will tell you {drum} talks so much in its arcades that the echoes have echoes.
{drum} thinks {nb} serves its food uncovered on purpose, to show it can afford to let the heat go.
{nb}'s children are told that in {drum} dropped cups fall spinward. They don't, and every child checks on their first glide.
Ask anyone in {nb} about {drum} and you'll hear about the broth, then the gin, then the broth again.
{drum} has never forgiven {nb} for calling its jook 'restful'.
According to {nb}, {drum} puts a lid on everything: the soup, the tea, the stew and any talk about its broth.
{drum} says {nb}'s baths are perfectly nice, and that a bath should never be perfectly nice. It should be too hot.
In {nb}, 'gone to {drum}' means gone to sulk somewhere with better broth.
{nb} claims {drum}'s ring counter drops the rice ball into the broth on purpose; {drum} says that is what a rice ball is for.
The joke in {nb} is that the only thing older than a {drum} chair is the argument about who sits in it.
In {nb} they say a tomato in {drum} gets its own plate and a short speech before anyone cuts it.
{drum} likes to point out that {nb}'s famous broth is only famous in {nb}.
{nb} sends its fussy eaters to {drum} for a week, and they come home eating the Nine off a spoon.
{nb} swears that if you leave a crock unattended in {drum}, someone will have fed it by morning.
{nb}'s Gate crews joke that {drum}'s Gate would sequence a sneeze if you held still long enough.
{drum} says {nb}'s Gate is friendly, which is not what anyone wants in a Gate.
{drum} says {nb} lights its corridors so brightly that you can't tell who's rich, which {nb} says is the idea.
{nb} reckons {drum} remembers every blight it ever had and cooks most of them again on purpose.
{drum} calls {nb}'s steaks 'young': from a line too new to have had a bad year.
{nb} says {drum} talks fast enough to make you check the helium, though it's the same air everywhere and {drum} just has more to say.
{nb}'s children are told that if they don't eat their Nine they'll be sent to {drum}, where it goes in the pudding.
{drum} and {nb} have argued about whose ring-counter broth is better for longer than either has kept records, and both are winning.
{nb} measures generosity in {drum} apples: half of one is a gift, and a whole one is a proposal.
{drum}'s grandmothers still say 'as bright as {nb}' about anything that costs too much.
{drum} says {nb}'s spinball players throw spinward to look strong, and then wonder why the ball dives.
{nb} likes to say that {drum} teaches its children to fly lengthwise and argue crosswise.
{nb} complains that {drum} has never once been on time, and {drum} says time is just a lamp setting.
{nb} still owes {drum} a crate of cheese from the Eleven Days, and both drums would like to keep it that way.
{drum}'s elders say {nb} ate its larder by the third day of the Eleven Days, and {nb}'s elders say {drum} had shared its own by the second.
{drum} says {nb} makes its Knotnight larder as if it expects to be rescued.
Every child in {nb} knows the first word a {drum} baby learns is 'anti', and the second is how to blame it on the drum.
{drum} says {nb} wears its clothes new, which seems a little sad, like a song nobody has learned yet.
{nb} has noticed that {drum} always dyes its linings the colour {nb} wore last year.
{drum} has one word for a guest from {nb}, and a warmer one for a guest from {nb} who brought herbs.
{drum} has decided that {nb}'s idea of a gift is a bottle of gin, and has been giving the same bottles back at weddings for decades.
{nb} jokes that {drum} glides over so often it should pay rent to the quay.
{nb} says {drum} is the only drum on {row} that applauds a good catch.
{nb} swears {drum}'s ring counter adds a pinch of the Nine if you look peaky.
In {nb} they say {drum}'s elders are too proud to glide and too curious to stay home, so they send their grandchildren with lists.
{drum} says {nb} gives herbs because it can't grow anything else, and {nb} says {drum} gives gin because it can't grow anything at all.
{nb} says {drum} keeps the oldest basil on {row} and talks to it more than to its neighbours.
{nb} glides over on {weekday}s for {drum}'s baths and stays for the arguments in the steam.
{nb} thinks {drum} wastes its Hollow hours on picnics, and {drum} says that is exactly what they are for.
According to {nb}, {drum}'s ring counter gives you the broth first and its opinion second, and both are free.
To {nb}, {drum}'s express travellers are easy to spot: five days poorer and still talking about it.
{drum} thinks {nb} rides the slow cycler just to show how much time it has.
{nb} swears {drum}'s cabs lean further than anyone's, and {drum} swears they lean exactly enough.
{drum} thinks {nb} dresses up for the Glide, which is a lot of effort for 140 seconds of falling.
{nb}'s platform crews say a car from {drum} always comes in singing, and leaves with one more song.
{nb} glides over just to see {drum}'s Spindle in the lamp-night, which looks like someone spilled a box of hand lamps down the middle.
{nb} claims {drum} paints even the inside of its lift cores, in case the cabs get bored.
{drum} says {nb}'s rooms ring like a bucket, and {nb} says {drum}'s felt swallows every joke whole.
{nb} says {drum} remembers the Eleven Days as if they'd lasted eleven years, and its larders prove it.
{nb} grumbles that {drum}'s Mill lager tastes of the Mill, and {drum} calls that honesty.
{drum} says it can spot a traveller from {nb} at the Gate: they declare their starter before anyone asks, then tell you its whole life.
{nb} says the only thing {drum} won't mend is its opinion of {nb}.
In {nb}, a 'lid-lifter' is someone from {drum}: they check every pot in the kitchen before they say hello.
{nb} has a name for a bath that goes on past dinner, and the name is {drum}.
{drum} admits {nb} has the better broth and the worse cups.
{nb} calls {drum} the place where good gin goes to be lectured about thiamine.
{drum} and {nb} agree on almost nothing, except that {far} makes terrible broth.
Every wanderer from {far} who passes through {drum} is told about {nb}'s broth, as a warning.
{nb} and {nb2} have argued for centuries about which of them {drum} likes best, and {drum} has never said.
{drum} sits between {nb} and {nb2} and has learned to agree with whichever one glided over last.
{nb} still talks about {name} from {drum}, who glided over to settle an argument about broth and stayed forty years.
{nb} has a theory that every block in {drum} believes it is the heart of the drum, and {block} has signs up to prove it.
{nb} says the elders' flats on deck {hdeck} of {drum} hold more opinions than the whole of {nb}.
{nb} knows {drum} will come to its weddings with a remade chair and go home with every recipe on the table.
{nb} insists that in {drum} even the arguments get mended and handed down.
{nb} swears {drum}'s children can catch a falling cup two centimetres antispinward without looking up.
The story in {nb} is that {drum} rotates its larder so carefully that the hard bread has a birthday.
{nb} says {drum} knows every leaf on its herb shelves by sight, and {drum} says {nb} would too if its basil were worth looking at.
{drum} says {nb}'s jook tastes as if a cooking robot had once heard jook described.
{nb} reckons {drum}'s flutes are so long the player is in one room and the tune is in the next.
{nb} says {drum} plays spinball like a debate: every throw anti, every point disputed.
{nb} calls {drum} 'the attic of {row}', because everything anyone ever threw away is in a {drum} flat, mended.
In {nb} they'll tell you {drum} re-dyes its coats for every festival, and you can read a coat's age in the colours left in its seams.
{nb} says {drum} takes its Hollow hour like medicine: on time, all of it, and with a face.
In {nb}, anyone who turns up to dinner with a whole apple is called 'a {drum} suitor'.
{nb} thinks {drum} is a lovely place for a long letter and a terrible place to keep a secret.
{nb} finds {drum} lovely and a little pleased with itself, and glides over most weeks to be sure.
{nb} says you can't sit down in {drum} without being given an aunt.
{nb} grumbles that {drum} pays six kays an hour for things {nb} does for nothing, like talking.
{nb} says {drum} mends its coats with the stitches on the outside, as if the holes were the good part.
{nb} calls {drum}'s block courts 'the weekly shout', and has quietly started one of its own.
{nb} jokes that {drum} reads its long letters aloud in the halls, so nobody there has had a private thought in years.
{drum}'s assembly by lot once drew a man who'd swapped in from {nb} the week before, and {nb} still claims the result.
{nb} sends its wanderers to {drum} first, so they learn to sit at a long table before they ride a long cycler.
Guest-right in {drum} is three nights, {nb} says, and the goodbyes take a fourth.
{drum}'s Ledger gets more readers from {nb} than {nb}'s own notices do.
{nb} glides over every Booking Day to watch {drum} read its Ledger, and pretends it has come for the feast.
{nb} says {drum} marries its young so early that the weddings come before the furniture.
{nb} says {drum} cheers its Margin on Booking Day even when it shrinks, which {nb} finds either very good or very odd.
To {nb}, {drum}'s Quiet is the loudest day on {row}: a whole drum gone dark, and every one of them in the halls talking.
{nb} says {drum}'s Homecoming is so loud that wanderers from {nb} get off at the wrong ring just to be met.
{nb} says you can't glide into {drum} without becoming a number on the Ledger and a name at somebody's table by dinner.
You can hear {drum}'s halls from the station ring, {nb} says, and {drum} says that's what a station ring is for.
{nb} says {drum} has never eaten a quiet meal, and {drum} has never wanted one.
{nb} claims {drum}'s choirs are so bright in the heliox they could strip paint, and {drum} has asked to borrow some paint.
{drum} says {nb} eats as if it were ashamed of it: alone, quickly, and standing up.
Nobody glides into {drum}, {nb} says, without being handed a bowl and a job.
{nb} says {drum} keeps four hundred seats at every long table and four hundred opinions about the ramen.
{nb} jokes that in {drum} even the libraries have a choir.
{nb} says {drum} feeds you three times, sings at you twice and teaches you something before you can get your coat on.
{nb} glides over on {weekday}s for {drum}'s hall dinners and comes home hoarse, which it calls a good night.
{drum} thinks {nb}'s idea of a crowd is three people and a cooking robot.
{nb} says {drum} is so quiet you can hear the pumps, and {drum} says that is the point.
Visitors from {nb} are easy to spot in {drum}'s woods: they're the ones whispering, as if a whisper didn't carry in heliox.
{nb} keeps a slate from {drum} on the wall of its ring counter. It says SHH, and nobody in {nb} has ever obeyed it.
In {nb} they say a conversation in {drum} takes a week and fits on one slate.
{drum} thinks {nb} talks the way other drums breathe: all the time and without noticing.
{nb} goes to {drum} to sulk, and {drum}'s woodwardens are very good at not asking why.
In {nb}, 'a {drum} answer' is one that arrives three days later, written down, and right.
{nb}'s children dare each other to sneeze in {drum}'s woods.
{nb} says {drum}'s woodwardens can tell who is in their wood by the particular way they aren't speaking.
{nb} sends its exhausted cooks to {drum} for a week of silence and gets them back calm, which unsettles everyone.
{nb} can't see {drum}'s dusks from 24.5 km away, but it hears about them for a week afterwards.
{nb} holds its weddings on {drum}'s terraces, because a {drum} dusk costs nothing and looks like a fortune.
{nb} suspects {drum} would paint the lamp-night too, if anyone let it.
{drum} calls {nb}'s dawns 'serviceable', which in {drum} is the cruellest word there is.
You can tell a {drum} child by the dye on their cuffs, {nb} says: a new colour every festival, the same cuffs since they were small.
{nb} says {drum} returns its rents to everyone, and everyone spends them on dye, so in the end the rents come back as coats.
{nb} pretends not to care about {drum}'s dawns, but half of {nb} glided over for {painter}'s last one.
{drum} says {nb} lights its Hollow like a kitchen: bright, even, and nothing to look at.
According to {nb}, {drum} throws a festival for anything, including the end of the last festival.
{nb} says a {drum} terrace seat costs a fortune at auction and pays you back on Booking Day, which {nb} has never quite understood.
{nb} warns its guests that {drum} can't pass a broken chair without fixing it, which makes visiting awkward.
{nb}'s word for anything handmade and a little too good is '{drum}-ish'.
{drum} says {nb} buys its best things in {drum} and forgets where they came from by the next glide.
Half the hand lamps flown in {nb}'s lamp-nights came from {drum}, and {drum} can tell which by the way they swing.
{nb} says {drum}'s apprentices are easy to spot: shavings in their hair and opinions about glue.
{nb} says {drum} will sell you anything except the thing you came for, which it will make for you, slowly.
{drum} has made {nb}'s wedding chairs for three hundred years, and still sends a note about the glue.
{nb} has learned that a gift from {drum} is never new and never finished: it comes with a spare part and a promise to come back and adjust it.
{nb} says {drum}'s makers sign their work so small you need a lamp and a grandmother to find it.
{nb} warns its wanderers that you can't stay three nights in {drum} without leaving with something half made.
{nb} says nothing ever happens in {drum}, which {drum} takes as the highest praise.
{nb} calls {drum} 'the sensible one', and glides there whenever it wants to be told off.
{nb} claims {drum}'s old Count board has been a noticeboard for so long that people pin lost gloves to it.
{nb} says {drum}'s idea of excitement is a new lining.
{drum} has kept the same rules for so long that {nb} uses them to settle bets.
{nb} likes to say {drum} is the drum you'd pick for the Eleven Days and the last you'd pick for a party.
{nb} says {drum} has stood at par so long that its children think 'par' is a kind of bread.
{drum} has kept the same ring-counter broth for four hundred years, {nb} says, and only argues about it on {weekday}s.
{nb} says you haven't eaten until you've eaten at a {drum} night market at two in the morning, when the kays are cheap and the noodles cheaper.
{nb} has more room than {drum}, and {drum} has more ideas about what a room is for.
{nb} says a {drum} flat is a bedroom at night, a kitchen at noon, a schoolroom by two and a choir by six.
{nb} admits that {drum} feeds people better on fewer kays than anywhere on {row}.
{drum} finds it a little sad that {nb}'s beds sit empty all day.
{nb} sends its students to {drum} to learn how to fold a bed into a wall and a table into a bed.
{nb} is sure {drum}'s swaps desk could find a flat for a whole choir by teatime.
{nb} would never say it in {drum}, but it is glad {drum} counts rather than breaks.
{nb} says {drum}'s Count is the only board on {row} that people cheer for going down.
{drum}'s young cooks feed half of {nb} on blight cheese, and {nb} has stopped pretending it comes for anything else.
{nb} glides over every Booking Day with tea for the crowd at {drum}'s Count board, and goes home with a bet on the date of par.
{nb} says {drum}'s fitting dinners are the best family meals on {row}, and wishes nobody needed them.

hollow.t: lawns that rise on either side until they hang overhead, where the far bank's picnics sit upside down
a great lawn mown in wide stripes, so from the far bank it looks ruled like a page
a chamomile lawn that gives off its scent when one deck's turn ends and the next walks across it
elders' benches along the main lawn, tilted back so you can watch the far bank without a stiff neck
a lawn on the midline where you can see both terraced end walls at once, nearly two kilometres either way
a running lap round the main lawn, where every race goes antispinward because that's the easy way
grass banks for rolling down, which takes half as long again at half a g and is better for it
a bowling green where a bowl sent spinward runs short and one sent antispinward runs long
a sloping lawn in the dim last stretch before the back wall, where couples go to be less seen
the far bank's lawns, three kilometres overhead and sharp enough to count the cups on a picnic cloth
a lake that holds part of the drum's water reserve, its level marked on a post by the jetty
a diving lake with a tower, where a dive takes half again as long to fall and everyone counts aloud
a narrow lake round a wooded island, reached by a footbridge children cross in four floating strides
a still lake that shows the far bank twice: overhead upside down, and in the water the right way up
a lake kept at bath warmth by the food plant's spare heat, full of elders at lamp-dawn
stepping stones across the lake's narrows, where children leap and come down a little spinward
a round lake in the middle of the floor, with the sunline lying across it in one bright stripe
a reed-fringed lake whose reeds are cut each year for paper and room screens
a lido of stone steps and warm benches, where elders swim slow lengths before the bright hours
a lake with five islands set like the seeds of an apple cut crosswise
a long thin lake down most of the floor's length, swum end to end once a year by the brave
a lake where people float on their backs and look straight up at the far bank's lake
a great lake filling a third of the floor, so a third of what hangs overhead is water
a lake that runs right round the floor in a band, so it hangs overhead as well as at your feet
a lake so wide that its far shore climbs the curve, and the swimmers out there seem to swim uphill
a broad lake holding a quarter of the drum's inside water, with orchard islands on it
a wide shallow lake you can wade across at half a g, knee-deep for a kilometre
more lake than lawn: half the floor is shallow water, and a Hollow hour here is mostly spent swimming
a swell lake whose paddles send waves in slow and tall, five seconds between crests
a children's swell, its waves tall enough to be serious and slow enough to be safe
a swell that only runs in the lamp-night, when kWh are cheapest, ridden by hand lamp
a paddle wall at the back of the lake, and a queue on the steps of people waiting to fall off slowly
a standing wave in a pumped channel below the end wall, ridden on boards by the boldest elders
a canal right round the floor, 9.4 kilometres of it, swum in relays on Booking Day
a narrow canal round the foot of each end wall, catching the water that falls from the terraces
a slow canal you can float down on your back from end wall to end wall in about an hour
a canal lined with herb beds that anyone may cut from on their Hollow hour
a canal fed warm from the food plant's loop, faintly steaming in the lamp-night
the main lawn at the turn of a deck's hour, one crowd going down as the next comes up
lakeside steps crowded at lamp-dawn, every bench taken by elders with towels
a floor so full in the bright hours that you can hear a dozen picnics at once in the ringing air
a crowded lake promenade where elders walk spinward on purpose, for the extra weight on their bones
paths wide enough for a whole deck to arrive at once, which it does at every change of turn
queues for the flying halls at both end walls, children in hired sleeves waiting under the nets
lamp-night picnics after the dusk ramp, hand lamps scattered all the way round to the far bank
the Spindle opened end to end after dusk, a slow drift of hand lamps along the axis
orchards on the brightest strip of the floor, whose trees get their light free from the sunline
apple orchards where every tree is numbered and every apple counted before it's picked
a pear orchard where school classes come with brushes to pollinate the blossom
an orchard of low-chill apples, one tree to each block, picked by lottery
cherry trees on the first terraces of the back wall, picked by children who jump for the high ones
espaliered pears along the foot of the end wall, where the light falls off and the fruit ripens slowly
a lemon and fig orchard on the floor's warmest strip, its lemons guarded like jewellery
an orchard where each tree was planted at a naming and still carries the child's name on a tag
an orchard on the far bank, its blossom hanging upside down over everyone's heads
a quince orchard whose fruit nobody eats raw and everyone makes into paste for the larder
orchard terraces stepped up the back wall, the top trees picked at a hop
a walnut and chestnut orchard whose nuts go to the halls for Knotnight
a beech wood whose canopy closes overhead, so the floor goes green and cool at full sun
a wood on the far bank, a dark patch overhead that people steer their walks by
a wood of mixed broadleaves planted three centuries ago, with paths that never quite run straight
a hazel coppice cut in rotation for kite spars, plant stakes and fencing
an oak wood with a woodwarden for every few hundred trees and a bench under each of the oldest
a wood of limes grown taller than they would at full weight, their crowns leaning over the paths
a wood of tall cedars planted when the drum was young, the oldest living things in it
a maple wood that drops a few leaves every day, since nothing tells it when to stop
a pine wood whose needles go into the halls' gin by the handful, though the Mill could make the taste
a dim wood kept at dusk-light all day, where people carry slates and say nothing
a dim wood of hollies and yews, its paths lit at ankle height in the lamp-night
a long dim wood down the middle of the floor, its canopy so close the sunline shows through in threads
a moss wood under shade cloth, kept dim and damp, where even a whisper carries
a dim strip of wood at the foot of the back wall, where the floor's light falls almost to nothing
a dim wood with a listening glade, a ring of stones where people sit and hear the drum's pumps
a bamboo wood that grows a hand's height a day and is cut for flutes, scaffolds and screens
a bamboo grove whose stems knock together when people brush past, ringing high in the heliox
a bamboo maze near the back wall, cut back a little differently every month
bamboo on the lower terraces of the end walls, grown tall and thin in the lighter weight
a bamboo wood with a path of split stems underfoot that clacks as you walk
a birch wood chilled one strip at a time, so somewhere in it the leaves are always turning yellow
a birch wood with white trunks so close together that the far bank shows through in stripes
a birch grove whose peeled bark is collected for paper, and a few long letters a year
a small birch wood on the far bank, a white smudge overhead that children point to
birches round the lake, their white trunks doubled in the water
an old yew wood so dark at full sun that people stop at its edge to let their eyes adjust
yew hedges clipped into green rooms, each with a bench and a gap for a door
a yew maze at the foot of the front wall, which children solve by leaping for a look over the top
a ring of yews round a quiet lawn where the year's dead are named on Booking Day
yews clipped into tall columns along the canal, older than the oldest chair in the drum
top terraces where a child can jump the height of a house, netted at the edge just in case
terrace gardens climbing the back wall, lighter each tier, until watering cans pour slowly
a third-g terrace laid out for leaping reels, where every leap lands a hand's width spinward
terraces let by the year to growers, whose tomatoes ripen slowly in the end wall's softer light
terraces where elders garden at a third of a g, because kneeling is easier when you weigh less
a stair of terraces planted with thyme and rosemary, so you can smell your way to the top
the top terraces, where a dropped trowel takes two seconds to land, a hand's width antispinward
terraces planted only with white flowers, which show from the far end of the Hollow at dusk
school terraces where every class keeps one bed and argues over who gets the light
terraces with ramps instead of stairs, so the old are pushed up in chairs that weigh less every tier
the elders' terrace on the back wall, with a long rail for leaning on to watch the painted dawn
strawberry terraces on the back wall, picked by children at a hop
a waterfall off the top terraces that starts slow and bends antispinward all the way down to its pool
vines trained down the terrace faces of the end walls, grapes hanging over each tier's edge
a long pergola of hops and grapes, cool and green through the brightest hours
kiwi vines over the cab pavilions, so the fruit hangs above the arrivals
a small vineyard on the floor's brightest strip, whose one barrel a year goes to weddings
climbing roses and clematis over every arch along the main path
passionflower vines climbing beside the Spindle lift, a little higher up the end wall every week
kite terraces at a third of a g, where a kite climbs at a walking pace
a kite lawn near the back wall where children fly kites up at the far bank
the top terraces on kite days, where a kite stays up on a slow stroll
a row of kite makers' stalls on the terraces, where you test a new kite by running with it
kites run over the main lawn all day by children in relays, a different block's colours each hour
bright paved squares with fountains whose jets come down a few paces spinward of where they rose
a big bright square for the Booking Day reading, with stone steps to sit on
a market square on the floor where terrace growers sell herbs by the bunch
a bright square laid out as a spinball court, with a stand for elders who shout about angles
a square of chalk drawings that the cleaning robots are set to steer round
the dancing square, paved smooth, where the music starts when the dusk ramp does
a mosaic square whose pattern only makes sense from the far bank
a square of water jets set in the paving, run through by children who dry off in minutes
bright squares at the middle of the floor, the most crowded and most lit place in the drum
a wildflower meadow cut once a year, its seed saved in paper twists by the schools
a long-grass meadow left uncut, where people lie hidden and look up at the far bank
a meadow of tall grass on the far bank that ripples overhead when a crowd walks through it
a meadow mown by hand once a year, on a day the elders turn out with scythes
a meadow mown into a new maze of paths every morning, solved by whoever comes up first
tall grasses round the lake, with paths trodden wherever people wanted them
a meadow on a broad terrace of the front wall, where you weigh a third of what you do at the rim
a children's meadow of long grass and dens, which nobody over twelve may mow
flower beds planted to bloom in turns, so some part of the floor is always in flower
a rose garden of old varieties whose names nobody can pronounce any more
flower borders along the main path, planted in the colours of this year's best dawn
a field of sunflowers, every head turned up at the sunline, since it never moves
lavender beds by the baths, cut each month for bath bags
a garden of night-scented flowers that open in the lamp-night, for walkers with hand lamps
a poppy field whose seed goes to the bakers
a flower clock whose beds open and close with the sunline's ramps
a cutting garden where anyone on their Hollow hour may take one stem home
beds of herbs and flowers mixed, so a wedding bouquet can also season the soup
cab pavilions among the trees, so you come up through the ground into shade before you look up
a bath pavilion at the water's edge, hot pools from the food plant's loop and the cold lake a step away
a music pavilion with a felt-lined roof, so the band carries instead of ringing
a tea pavilion on stilts over the water, where every cup comes lidded
the elders' pavilion by the lake, with first claim on the shade at full sun
a long dining pavilion where whole decks eat together on their Hollow turn
a pavilion for sleeping through the bright hours, hung with felt and kept at dusk-light
a chess pavilion where games are left mid-move for whichever deck comes up next
small white pavilions scattered across the far bank, their roofs overhead like dropped dice
a dance pavilion with a sprung floor, packed for the reel that ends each Hollow turn
a puppet pavilion on the lawns, its shows timed to finish before the dusk ramp

dawns.name: The River
dawns.note: Oona's: the brown-violet of the River's dusty edge, warming through rose, with the far bank gold for twenty minutes while the near side is still dark.

dawns.name: Green dusk
dawns.note: Hesk's: forty minutes of cold sea-green as the sunline goes out, the far bank turning blue-black overhead.

dawns.name: Bruise
dawns.note: The back crews' word for the River's dust lanes, played as a dusk: white to mauve to a brown-violet you can almost feel.

dawns.name: Pewter
dawns.note: Nothing but greys, lifting so evenly that nobody can say when it became morning.

dawns.name: Apricot
dawns.note: The first ramp every lamp-painting school teaches: brown, apricot, cream, and no surprises.

dawns.name: Strong tea
dawns.note: Steeps from pale gold to the brown of tea left standing, then to the bottom of the cup.

dawns.name: Court pear
dawns.note: Green-gold like the espaliered pears, for the morning the children take their brushes to the blossom.

dawns.name: Ice
dawns.note: A cold blue morning that makes the baths feel hotter; bath-keepers ask for it.

dawns.name: Ember
dawns.note: Goes out red and slow, the way a lamp filament cools after the switch.

dawns.name: Lilac-grey
dawns.note: Soft violet greys, often chosen for the morning after a funeral.

dawns.name: Saffron
dawns.note: Deep yellow from the first minute, bright and a little brash. Children love it.

dawns.name: Mint
dawns.note: Cool greens with a white finish, played on the first morning after a blight lifts.

dawns.name: Plum
dawns.note: Plum to wine to dark: a wedding dusk, slow enough to dance through.

dawns.name: Keel copper
dawns.note: Copper and brass, by a pipe-fitter's daughter who said the Keel's plumbing was the best thing she had ever seen.

dawns.name: Celadon
dawns.note: The grey-green of an old glaze, almost unchanging for the first hour.

dawns.name: Persimmon
dawns.note: A loud orange morning, the sort fair drums save for festival days.

dawns.name: Indigo
dawns.note: Down through blue into indigo, done before the night markets open.

dawns.name: Linen
dawns.note: Undyed colours, grey-brown, oatmeal and linen, which elders ask for by name.

dawns.name: Rhubarb
dawns.note: Pink and sharp, like the stalks the Garden sells by the finger.

dawns.name: Slate and rose
dawns.note: Grey for two hours, then rose all at once, which some people find rude.

dawns.name: Verdigris
dawns.note: Blue-green like an old bell's patina, fading out under the far bank.

dawns.name: Mill caramel
dawns.note: Thick amber, the colour of Mill caramel held up to a lamp.

dawns.name: Lavender
dawns.note: Blue-violet to white, written for a choir's hundredth year.

dawns.name: Madder red
dawns.note: A red ground on Pigment Row, darkening to wine before the lamp-night.

dawns.name: Quince
dawns.note: Yellow with a grey-green underneath, slow at first and then quick.

dawns.name: Ink
dawns.note: Blue-grey to ink, as plain as a long letter.

dawns.name: Rice
dawns.note: Very nearly colourless, warm grey to the white of cooked rice. A quiet painter's morning.

dawns.name: Moss
dawns.note: Dark moss warming to pale leaf, for drums that like their mornings dim.

dawns.name: Cinnabar
dawns.note: A hard red-orange that arrives too early and is gone by full sun.

dawns.name: Heather
dawns.note: Purple-grey and soft at the edges, like a coat re-dyed one time too many.

dawns.name: Lemon
dawns.note: Sharp yellow, clean as a cut lemon, painted on a bet and kept.

dawns.name: Blue hour
dawns.note: White through lilac into one long blue, the last of it lasting most of an hour.

dawns.name: Peach
dawns.note: Warm and soft-edged, the easiest dawn on the calendar to sleep through.

dawns.name: Graphite
dawns.note: Pencil greys warming to cream, drawn rather than painted.

dawns.name: Teal
dawns.note: Bright teal at the turn, then deep-water colours, then dark.

dawns.name: Slate and marigold
dawns.note: Slate-blue for most of the ramp, then a marigold edge that reaches the far bank ten minutes before the floor.

dawns.name: Tomato
dawns.note: The dearest-looking morning on the row: tomato red, which costs exactly what grey does.

dawns.name: Pistachio
dawns.note: Pale nut-green and gentle, a favourite for school mornings.

dawns.name: Mulberry
dawns.note: Purple and stained, ending in a near-black that keeps a hint of red.

dawns.name: Steel
dawns.note: Cool blue-greys, very even, for working days.

dawns.name: Slow caramel
dawns.note: Brown-gold slipping to brown, the colour of something left all night on the 65-degree loop.

dawns.name: Coral
dawns.note: Pink-orange and warm, and a little too pleased with itself.

dawns.name: Jade
dawns.note: Clear green to white, made to set a dim wood's yews glowing.

dawns.name: Fig
dawns.note: Dusty purple-brown, soft as the inside of a fig.

dawns.name: Ultramarine
dawns.note: Strong blue to deep blue, with no grey in it anywhere.

dawns.name: Matcha
dawns.note: Grass-green and bitter-bright, played on the tea-blenders' day.

dawns.name: Butter
dawns.note: Soft yellow on cream, the colour of cultured butter on warm bread.

dawns.name: Pale blue
dawns.note: A clean blue-white morning that makes the far bank look close enough to touch.

dawns.name: Rust
dawns.note: Red-brown and gritty, like old iron on the back of a radiator panel.

dawns.name: Pomegranate
dawns.note: Deep red to pink to white, much asked for at namings.

dawns.name: Sage
dawns.note: Grey-green and calm: the herb-shelf colour.

dawns.name: Dusk rose
dawns.note: Old rose fading through mauve, the most requested dusk on more than one row.

dawns.name: Bottle glass
dawns.note: Green as old glass, painted so the light seems to come through water.

dawns.name: Tamarind
dawns.note: Sour brown-orange, then brown, then a warm dark.

dawns.name: Periwinkle
dawns.note: Blue with violet in it, gentle and cool.

dawns.name: Booking gold
dawns.note: All gold, and quickly, for the morning the beam is booked.

dawns.name: Wine
dawns.note: A dark red dusk for the evening of a wedding, when nobody is watching the sunline anyway.

dawns.name: Olive
dawns.note: Olive and khaki, unfashionable and much loved.

dawns.name: Cobalt
dawns.note: A clear blue that goes on getting bluer until it's dark.

dawns.name: Raspberry
dawns.note: Hot pink and unapologetic, by an eleven-year-old who won the school's painting lottery.

dawns.name: Lilac
dawns.note: Pale purple with nothing sad in it.

dawns.name: Bronze
dawns.note: Warm metal tones closing over the Hollow like a lid.

dawns.name: Lake and coral
dawns.note: Blue-green water colours warming to coral at the top: a swimmers' dawn.

dawns.name: Mauve
dawns.note: Grey-pink to grey-purple, very quiet.

dawns.name: Barley
dawns.note: Pale straw and oatmeal: a baker's dawn.

dawns.name: Ink and cherry
dawns.note: Bright red falling through wine into blue-black, short and dramatic.

dawns.name: Cold milk
dawns.note: Grey-blue to a bluish white, as plain as a cup of milk.

dawns.name: Oolong
dawns.note: Green-gold and amber, like tea in a glass.

dawns.name: Cornflower
dawns.note: Clear mid-blue, chosen for the morning the terrace kites go up.

dawns.name: Ochre
dawns.note: Yellow earth from Pigment Row, then cream.

dawns.name: Umber
dawns.note: Brown earth tones, closing slowly and without fuss.

dawns.name: Lapis
dawns.note: Deep blue under a warm white, like the gold flecks in the stone.

dawns.name: Malachite
dawns.note: Banded greens, strong and cool.

dawns.name: Violet and saffron
dawns.note: Starts violet and turns yellow in one long stroke. The painter called it a quarrel that made up.

dawns.name: Rose and teal
dawns.note: Teal underneath and rose on top, the two never quite mixing.

dawns.name: Pear and plum
dawns.note: Pale pear-yellow giving way to plum, after the two old trees in a block's Court.

dawns.name: Long grey
dawns.note: Three hours of grey with the faintest warmth at the end, chosen for the Quiet.

dawns.name: Long Flight
dawns.note: The dusk before the Long Flight, ending in a dark so deep that the first hand lamps on the Spindle look like a slow river.

dawns.name: Knotnight
dawns.note: Grey-violet and early, for the evening the lamps go down and the larder is made.

dawns.name: Homecoming
dawns.note: Warm and quick and a little sentimental, for the morning the wanderers come home.

dawns.name: Naming
dawns.note: Soft pink-gold, made for a family who wanted a dawn the baby wouldn't mind.

dawns.name: Shutter
dawns.note: Twenty minutes of red-black before anything happens, like the wait before a Window opens.

dawns.name: Visor
dawns.note: By a retired back-crew hand: suit-visor amber fading to the dark behind the radiators.

dawns.name: Occultation
dawns.note: Gold that goes out from one edge, the way a star does when a raft's edge crosses it.

dawns.name: Crosswise
dawns.note: Skin green to cut red to the cream of the flesh: an apple, for weddings.

dawns.name: Black garlic
dawns.note: Sweet browns going to near-black, for the cooks who keep the loop.

dawns.name: Jook
dawns.note: White on white on white, a joke for a hall that serves jook at lamp-dawn.

dawns.name: Chilli oil
dawns.note: Red with a gloss on it, darkening fast.

dawns.name: Shiso
dawns.note: Purple leaf turning green, after the herb on every shelf.

dawns.name: Far bank first
dawns.note: A dusk that darkens the far bank first, so the people overhead reach the night before you do.

dawns.name: Lime
dawns.note: Acid green, very fast, for a drum that likes to be woken properly.

dawns.name: Halfway
dawns.note: Stops halfway for ten minutes so the terraces can take it in, then finishes.

dawns.name: Selkie
dawns.note: Painted during a Passing, from a colour Selkie's choirs described in a song that arrived thirty-three minutes after the question.

dawns.name: Hall lamps
dawns.note: Dims through the warm yellow of the halls' lamps, so the Hollow seems to go indoors before it goes dark.

dawns.name: Night garden
dawns.note: Blue-green shadows under a cool white, for evenings when the gardens stay open late.

dawns.name: Pewter and gold
dawns.note: Grey that turns to gold only in the last half hour, like a good speech.

dawns.name: Bamboo
dawns.note: Yellow-green and upright, with the far bank's colour arriving a beat before the floor's.

mottos: What fell from the River, we keep.
Last to go dark: the herbs.
Light is dear; colour is free.
Take a spoon, leave a spoon.
Slow and tall, like the waves.
Under the far bank, we're all upside down.
Kays come and go; chairs stay.
Felt on the ceiling, peace at the table.
Light the Court, feed the pears.
Eleven days, and the Glide still ran.
The beam comes; we make the rest.
Spend the hour on each other.
A Hollow hour is a gift.
Low and slow, on the loop.
The drum turns; we needn't hurry.
Once at eight, for ever after.
Named for the dead, raised by the living.
Mass is dear; time is cheap.
If it fell, it fell anti.
Wrap the pears, wait for the bloom.
Rank behind rank, and all of them home.
A drum is a long table.
The oldest chair for the guest.
Pull up a chair, any chair.
Salad on Sundays, pastry every day.
Leave the lamp on for the basil.
We are what we didn't throw away.
The quay lights go on for ever.
The Glide is free, and so are you.
